---
title: "From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)"
subtitle: "Seventy years of action and reaction: how the forward pass went from a gamble to a weapon, how the defense answered every new offense, and why by 1977 almost nobody could score."
description: "The first half of football's arms race, told as action and reaction: the forward pass legalized in 1906 and hedged with penalties; Pop Warner's single wing and its direct snap; the T-formation's 73–0 arrival in 1940; platoon football and the specialist; Paul Brown's playbooks, film study and messenger guards; Steve Owen's umbrella defense and Tom Landry's 4-3 and Flex; Lombardi's power sweep; Sid Gillman's vertical passing; the AFL as a passing laboratory and the 1966–70 merger; Red Hickey's 1960 shotgun; and the 1970s scoring drought, with the 1972 and 1974 rule changes that failed to end it."
glossary:
  "Single wing": "A direct-snap formation that dominated football from the 1910s into the 1940s: an unbalanced line, a tailback four to five yards deep who took the snap through the air and could run, pass or hand off, a fullback beside him, a blocking back near the line and a wingback just outside the end. The ancestor of the shotgun and the wildcat."
  "Platoon football": "Using separate groups of players for offense and defense (later also for special teams and for particular situations), which became possible once the rules allowed free substitution: permanently in the NFL from 1950. Before it, the same eleven men played both ways."
  "Umbrella defense": "Steve Owen's New York Giants defense of 1950: a 6-1-4 alignment (six linemen, one linebacker, four defensive backs) whose two ends could drop into pass coverage after the snap, so against a pass it became a 4-1-6. Built to stop Paul Brown's Cleveland Browns; one of the ancestors of the 4-3."
  "Flex defense": "Tom Landry's Dallas Cowboys version of the 4-3, from the mid-1960s: two of the four defensive linemen line up a yard or so off the ball, read the blocks, then fill an assigned gap, so that every gap has an owner. Built to stop 'run to daylight' running games like Vince Lombardi's."
  "AFL": {def: "The American Football League (1960–1969), the rival league that played a more wide-open passing game, introduced the two-point conversion and won two of the four AFL–NFL Super Bowls before merging with the NFL (agreement 1966, complete 1970). Its ten teams became the core of today's AFC.", aliases: ["American Football League"]}
  "Chuck rule": "Any of the rules limiting how a defender may hit or shove (chuck) a receiver who is running his route. From 1974, only once after the receiver was 3 yards past the line; from 1977, only once in all; since 1978, only within 5 yards of the line (the Mel Blount rule)."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers)"
#| output: false
import os
import shutil
import textwrap

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style
from gridiron.formations import LINE_D, OFF_BALL, OL_SPLIT, TE_W

style.apply()

UC = -1.9                      # quarterback under center (drawn a little off the ball)
BACK_RING = style.THIRD        # aqua ring: the ball carrier or the back to watch
KEY_RING = style.DEFENSE       # orange ring: the defender to watch
THREAT = "#0f7a55"             # darker aqua for "the back could go here" arrows (safe for text)


def P(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    """Offensive player at (d, w): d = yards from the ball (negative = backfield), w = yards to the offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def OL(key, w, label=""):
    """An offensive lineman on the line; only the center gets a letter."""
    return Player(key, "OL", "off", LINE_D, w, label=label)


def line5(split=OL_SPLIT):
    return [OL("LT", -2 * split), OL("LG", -split), OL("C", 0.0, "C"), OL("RG", split), OL("RT", 2 * split)]


def check_legal(players):
    """Seven offensive players on the line, and only the two at its ends may be receivers."""
    off = [q for q in players if q.side == "off"]
    on = sorted([q for q in off if q.d > -1.0], key=lambda q: q.w)
    assert len(on) == 7, [q.key for q in on]
    for q in on[1:-1]:
        assert q.pos == "OL", f"covered receiver {q.key}"
    assert len(off) == 11, len(off)
    return players


def hide_yard_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the faint painted field numbers (they sit where wide players stand in zoomed plates)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() is not None and abs(t.get_alpha() - 0.55) < 1e-6:
            t.remove()


def XY(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def draw_play(p, lateral, window, width_in=6.5):
    """Draw a play edge to edge at `width_in` (Play.draw's own figure leaves wide empty margins)."""
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.004, right=0.996, top=0.996, bottom=0.004)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    return fld


def label(fld, p, text, at, target=None, ha="center", fs=7.2, color=style.INK, va="center"):
    """A short boxed label at (d, w); with `target`, a thin leader line to that spot."""
    x, y = XY(fld, p, *at)
    box = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6)
    if target is None:
        fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, ha=ha, va=va, color=color, zorder=12, bbox=box)
    else:
        tx, ty = XY(fld, p, *target)
        fld.ax.annotate(text, xy=(tx, ty), xytext=(x, y), fontsize=fs, ha=ha, va=va, color=color, zorder=12,
                        bbox=box, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=7))


def dashed_arrow(fld, p, pts, color=THREAT, lw=1.6, z=6, head=10):
    """A dashed arrow through absolute (d, w) points: an option, a fake, or the flight of a direct snap."""
    xs, ys = XY(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=z)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2] + 0.7 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.7 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])),
                                     (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color,
                                     lw=lw, zorder=z))


def gap_mark(fld, p, w, text, d=-0.15, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK):
    """A small gap letter sitting on the line of scrimmage between two blockers."""
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=6.6, ha="center", va="center", color=color, fontweight="bold", zorder=9,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=0.6))


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web), cropped to the part of the field that matters -------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), mark_r=MARK_R):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, trails, optional rings (key, color)."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.8, play.los + window[1] - 0.8)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.8, yhi - 0.8)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x + 0.75, y + 0.55), 0.6, 0.36, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), mark_r, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=mark_r * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (mark_r / MARK_R) * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.7 * mark_r, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=9))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.5, mark_r=MARK_R, extra=None):
    """Numbered frame strip with a fixed window and a note under each frame.
    `extra(fld, i)`, if given, draws on frame i (0-based) after the players."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.62 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        fld = panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, mark_r)
        if extra is not None:
            extra(fld, i)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.2,
                    color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), width_in=5.2, mark_r=MARK_R, extra=None):
    """Web version of the strip: the same panel at every frame, with the strip's notes as captions."""
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, mark_r)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(play, times, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        kw.pop("ncols", None)
        video(play, times, **kw)
```

Watch an NFL game today and sooner or later a running back walks up behind the center, five
yards deep, with the quarterback split out wide like a receiver. The center snaps the ball through
the air straight to the back, an extra lineman stands on one side of the line, and a second back is
already sprinting across the formation. The broadcaster calls it the *wildcat* and treats it as a
gimmick. A fan from 1935 would call it Saturday: it is the single wing, the formation football was
built on. Now jump to 1977. NFL teams scored 17.2 points a game that season, the fewest since 1942,
and not one receiver in the league reached 1,000 yards. How did football get from the single wing to
the T-formation to the pro passing games of the 1960s, and then, with all that passing knowledge,
grind to a near-halt? This chapter is the first half of that story, told the way it happened: every
offensive idea, the defense's answer, and the rules that tilted the board.

**You'll be able to…**

- Explain why the forward pass, legal since 1906, took decades to become a real weapon, and name the
  rules that made it risky.
- Recognize the single wing and the T-formation, and say why the T replaced the single wing within a
  decade of the Chicago Bears' 73–0 win in 1940.
- Describe what Paul Brown and platoon football changed about how teams are organized, coached and
  play-called, and why that model is still the default.
- Trace today's 4-3 to its ancestors (Steve Owen's umbrella defense, Tom Landry's 4-3 and his Flex)
  and say which offense each was built to stop: Brown's passing, Lombardi's sweep.
- Explain the AFL as a passing laboratory (Sid Gillman, Hank Stram), the 1960 shotgun, and the merger.
- Read the points-per-game record from 1932 to 1977 and explain why scoring fell in the 1970s (and not
  earlier), and why the rule changes of 1972, 1974 and 1977 didn't fix it when 1978's did.

## Reading this part: action and reaction

Every chapter so far has met a scheme in its present form and given it a short history sidebar. This
part of the book connects those sidebars into one story, and the story has a shape: **an offense finds
an advantage, the defense builds an answer, and when the defense gets too far ahead, the rule-makers
step in.** The single wing was football's answer to a game with almost no passing. The T answered the
single wing's slowness. Platoons and Paul Brown made the T a specialist's offense. The umbrella and
the 4-3 answered Brown's passes; the Flex answered Lombardi's runs. The AFL (the American Football
League, a rival league of the 1960s) went looking for points in the passing game, and by the 1970s the defenses had caught up with everyone. Hold on to that rhythm
and the dates take care of themselves.

## 1906: a pass nobody wanted to throw

Football in 1905 was a shoving match. The ball was snapped, and the offense's whole team crashed into
the defense in a mass, with ball carriers pushed and pulled forward by their own teammates. That
season, by the count usually cited, 19 players died nationwide, and President Theodore Roosevelt, a fan
who wanted the game saved rather than banned, pressed the colleges to reform it. Among the changes the
rules committee adopted on April 6, 1906, was one meant to spread the players out: **the forward pass
became legal.**[^pass1906]

It was legal, but nobody wanted to throw it, and the reason was the rulebook. The early rules made a
pass a gamble with lopsided odds. A pass that hit the ground untouched could cost the offense the ball
(from 1907, a 15-yard penalty instead), it had to cross the line of scrimmage at least five yards to
either side of the center, and a pass caught in the end zone was not a touchdown but a touchback. Some
early versions also limited how far downfield a pass could be caught. Think about that as a coach: a
run that fails costs you a down; a pass that fails can cost you the ball. Most coaches ran.

The rules eased slowly. In 1912 the colleges added the 10-yard end zone, a fourth down and the
six-point touchdown, and dropped the limit on how far a pass could travel. A year later a small
Catholic school from Indiana, Notre Dame, beat Army at West Point by throwing the ball around, with Gus
Dorais passing to an end named Knute Rockne; the two had practiced it on a beach the summer before,
while working as lifeguards. Newspapers loved it. Coaches mostly didn't change.[^early]

The professional league that became the NFL was founded in 1920 and took its rules from the colleges,
and for its first dozen years it played the same cautious, running game. Two rule changes in 1933 and
1934 finally made the pass a normal play. The trigger was a controversial touchdown in the 1932 playoff
game, played indoors on a shortened field because of a blizzard: Chicago's Bronko Nagurski faked a run,
backed up a step and threw a short touchdown pass, and Portsmouth argued that he hadn't been the
required five yards behind the line. For 1933 the NFL broke with the college rulebook and **allowed a
forward pass from anywhere behind the line of scrimmage**. The same off-season it added [hash
marks](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) (lines in the field from which every
play starts, so the ball was no longer spotted beside the sideline) and moved the goalposts up to the
goal line to encourage field goals. And from 1934, **a second incomplete pass in the same set of downs no longer cost
five yards**.[^nfl1933] Meanwhile the ball itself got slimmer through the 1920s and '30s, easier to grip
and spiral.

You can see the effect in the scoring. In 1932 an NFL team scored 8.2 points a game; by 1948 it was
23.2, close to three times as many (the points chart later in this chapter shows the whole curve). The
pass was not the only cause, since the T-formation and free substitution arrived in the same years
(both are coming up), and the season-by-season passing numbers for the 1930s are too patchy to split the
credit. But the direction is clear: by the peak years of the 1950s and '60s, NFL teams threw on about
half their plays.[^passrate] Offenses needed a player who could throw.

## The single wing: power and deception from a direct snap

For the first decades of the forward pass, the formation that ran football was the [**single
wing**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-single-wing). It is usually credited to Glenn "Pop" Warner at
the Carlisle Indian Industrial School around 1907, where Jim Thorpe played tailback for him; Warner
called it the Carlisle formation, and the name *single wing* came later from the one "wing" back
lined up outside the end.[^singlewing]

```{python}
#| label: fig-single-wing
#| fig-cap: "The single wing (strength to the offense's right; an illustrative alignment, since depths varied by team). The line is unbalanced: four men to the right of the center (both guards, a tackle and the end) and only two (a tackle and the end) to its left, so the play side has more blockers than a balanced line. This is the guard-over version; many teams moved a tackle over instead. Seven men are on the line, and the two at its ends (E) are eligible. There is no quarterback under center: the center snaps the ball through the air (dashed brown) to the tailback (T, aqua ring) about five yards deep, who can run, pass or hand off. The fullback (F) stands beside him, the blocking back (B), called the quarterback in its day, just behind the line, and the wingback (W) a yard off the line outside the right end."
def single_wing():
    return check_legal([
        P("WE", "TE", LINE_D, -3.2, "E"), OL("WT", -1.6), OL("C", 0.0, "C"), OL("WG", 1.6), OL("SG", 3.2),
        OL("ST", 4.8), P("SE", "TE", LINE_D, 6.4, "E"),
        P("QB", "TB", -5.0, 0.6, "T"), P("FB", "FB", -4.4, 2.8, "F"), P("BB", "HB", -2.1, 4.0, "B"),
        P("WB", "HB", -1.6, 8.3, "W")])


sw = Play(single_wing(), None, los=40, to_go=None)
sw.highlight("QB", color=BACK_RING)
fld = draw_play(sw, lateral=(-16.0, 18.0), window=(-10.5, 5.8))
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, sw, 0.0, 0.0), XY(fld, sw, -4.2, 0.55)
fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9, color=style.BALL,
                                 lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=5, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25"))
label(fld, sw, "unbalanced line: four men to the right\nof the center, two to the left", (3.7, -5.4))
label(fld, sw, "wingback (W): a yard off\nthe line, outside the end", (3.7, 11.6), target=(-1.6, 8.3))
label(fld, sw, "tailback (T): takes the snap about\n5 yards deep; runs, passes or hands off",
      (-8.6, -6.6), target=(-5.0, 0.6))
label(fld, sw, "direct snap: the ball\nflies back to him", (-2.8, -8.2), target=(-2.4, 0.35))
label(fld, sw, "fullback (F): fakes,\nspins or runs", (-8.6, 8.4), target=(-4.4, 2.8))
label(fld, sw, "blocking back (B):\nthe lead blocker", (-4.4, 12.4), target=(-2.1, 4.0))
plt.show()
```

Read it from the back, the way [Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd)
taught you to read any formation. There's no one under center. The **tailback**, the star, stands
four or five yards deep and takes a **direct snap**, a long toss between the center's legs. Beside him is
the **fullback**, a power runner and faker. Up near the line is the **blocking back**, who was called
the quarterback but almost never threw: his job was to lead the play and call the signals. And just
outside the end is the **wingback**, a runner on reverses and a receiver on passes. The line is
**unbalanced**: one lineman from the weak side moves over to the strong side, so four players stand to
the right of the center and only two, a tackle and an end, to its left. In the picture it's a guard
(both guards, a tackle and the end on the right); many teams moved a tackle over instead, which made the
strong side guard, tackle, tackle, end. Either way the point was the same.

### Why it existed

The single wing was built for a game in which the run was everything and the pass was an occasional
surprise, and it solved that game's problems well.

**More blockers than the defense had defenders at the point of attack.** Look at the right side of the
line in the picture: both guards, a tackle and the end, the wingback and the blocking back, plus the
fullback, all on one side. The signature play, the off-tackle power, sent nearly all of them at one spot,
and the formation was built so that the key defender there could be double-teamed.

**A runner who could also throw.** Because the tailback caught the snap standing up, five yards deep,
every run started as a possible pass, and every pass as a possible run. The great tailbacks were
*triple-threat* players: they could run, pass and punt, which in the low-scoring game of the era was
as valuable as anything else they did.

**Deception from the backfield.** With the ball snapped to either deep back, the backs could spin,
fake and hand off behind the line. The single wing's *spinner* plays (the fullback takes the snap,
turns his back to the defense and either keeps it or hands to a back circling behind him) and its
reverses to the wingback were built to make the defense guess.

A note on the letters in the next three pictures. They show the defenses of the 1930s and '40s, which
used the era's names: **E** end, **T** tackle, **G** guard, **L** linebacker, **H** halfback (a
defensive back), **S** safety. Defenders are always orange squares and offensive players blue circles,
so a blue **T** is the single wing's tailback and an orange **T** is a defensive tackle. From the
Lombardi section on, the 4-3 letters of [Part 5](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd)
take over: **S**, **M** and **W** are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, and the safeties are **FS** and
**SS**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-single-wing-power
#| fig-cap: "The single wing's bread-and-butter play, the off-tackle power to the strong side, against a six-man front of the era (six linemen, two linebackers L, two defensive halfbacks H and a safety; an illustrative reconstruction; the far-side halfback and the safety are beyond the top and left of the picture). (1) Count before the snap: right of the ball the offense has seven blockers (shaded) against five defenders. (2) The snap has flown back to the tailback (T, aqua ring). The right end and the wingback double-team the defensive tackle (orange T), the blocking back (B) kicks out the defensive end (E), and the inside guard (G, dark ring), the one next to the center, pulls behind the line to lead. (3) The fullback (F) and the guard lead through the hole onto the linebacker and the halfback. (4) The tailback follows his blockers off the tackle's outside hip."
def era_six_man():
    """A six-man front of the 1930s, shifted toward the single wing's strong (right) side."""
    return [D("DE_L", "DE", 1.3, -5.0, "E"), D("DT_L", "DT", 1.3, -2.4, "T"),
            D("DG_L", "DT", 1.3, 0.3, "G"), D("DG_R", "DT", 1.3, 3.0, "G"),
            D("DT_R", "DT", 1.3, 5.6, "T"), D("DE_R", "DE", 1.3, 9.0, "E"),
            D("LB_L", "LB", 4.0, -0.6, "L"), D("LB_R", "LB", 4.0, 5.0, "L"),
            D("HB_L", "DB", 8.0, -11.5, "H"), D("HB_R", "DB", 7.5, 11.6, "H"), D("S", "S", 13.5, 1.5, "S")]


sw_pw = [OL("WG", 1.6, "G") if q.key == "WG" else q for q in single_wing()]
pw = Play(sw_pw, era_six_man(), los=40, to_go=None)
# the defense reacts first (blocks aim at where these men end up)
pw.path("DT_R", [(2.2, 4.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.15, speed=1.6)     # driven inside by the double team
pw.path("DE_R", [(0.8, 9.9)], absolute=True, delay=0.1, speed=2.5)      # steps upfield, gets kicked out
pw.path("LB_R", [(3.2, 6.9)], absolute=True, delay=0.45, speed=3.0)     # fills the hole
pw.path("LB_L", [(3.2, 1.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.45, speed=3.0)
pw.path("HB_R", [(6.0, 10.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.6, speed=4.0)
pw.path("S", [(10.0, 6.5)], absolute=True, delay=0.6, speed=4.5)
# the blocks
pw.block("SE", pts=[(2.6, -0.5)], speed=2.2)                  # end: down on the tackle
pw.block("WB", pts=[(2.2, -2.6)], speed=2.6)                  # wingback: the other half of the double team
pw.block("ST", target="DG_R", speed=2.0)
pw.block("C", target="DG_L", speed=2.0)
pw.block("WT", target="DT_L", speed=2.0)
pw.block("SG", target="LB_L", speed=3.0)
pw.block("BB", target="DE_R", speed=4.0)                      # blocking back: the kick-out
pw.block("FB", pts=[(2.4, 2.4), (6.4, 4.6)], speed=5.5, delay=0.2)    # fullback: lead through the hole
pw.pull("WG", [(-1.2, 0.4), (-1.5, 3.6), (0.9, 5.6), (5.2, 8.8)], speed=5.2)  # inside guard pulls and leads
pw.run("QB", [(-4.6, 2.2), (-2.8, 5.4), (0.2, 7.5), (3.0, 8.4), (7.0, 8.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.45,
       speed=7.0)


def count_panel(fld, i):
    """Frame 1 only: shade the strong side and count blockers against defenders."""
    if i != 0:
        return
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = XY(fld, pw, -5.9, 0.9), XY(fld, pw, 8.6, 13.1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(xa, xb), min(ya, yb)), abs(xb - xa), abs(yb - ya), fc=style.OFFENSE,
                               alpha=0.07, ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=0.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=0.6))
    label(fld, pw, "right of the ball:\n7 blockers, 5 defenders", (6.6, 5.6), fs=6.8)


animation_or_strip(pw, [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.6], lateral=(-6.0, 13.5), window=(-6.3, 9.3),
                   rings=[("QB", BACK_RING), ("WG", style.OFFENSE_DARK)], mark_r=0.58, extra=count_panel,
                   notes=["count: seven blockers\nto five defenders",
                          "double team, kick-out;\nthe inside guard (G) pulls",
                          "fullback and guard lead\nthrough the hole",
                          "the tailback follows\nhis blockers"])
```

### What it gave up

Everything in the single wing was slow. The snap traveled five yards through the air before anything
could happen, the tailback started from a standstill, and the play took a long time to reach the line.
The defense could see who had the ball; it couldn't always see what he would do with it, but it knew
where to look. And the formation demanded one extraordinary athlete: a tailback who ran, passed, punted
and often played defense too. A team without one had no offense.

The defenses of the era matched it man for man. Six or seven linemen stood shoulder to shoulder, with
one or two linebackers behind them and three defensive backs, as in the picture: a run defense with a
little pass insurance.

## 1940: 73–0 and the T's takeover

The T-formation was older than the single wing. What was new in 1940 was a version of it that worked.
[Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd#the-ancestor-the-t-formation)
drew the [T-formation](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd) and explained its
logic: the quarterback's hands under the center, an instant snap, backs who hit the line at full
speed, and a ball handler who can fake to one back and give to another with his back to the defense.
Here is how it took over.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sw-vs-t
#| fig-cap: "The two formations side by side, at the same scale (illustrative alignments). Left, the single wing: an unbalanced line, the ball snapped through the air to a tailback (T, aqua ring) about five yards deep, and three backs stacked to the strong side. Right, the T: a balanced line, the quarterback (Q, aqua ring) with his hands under the center, and three backs in a row about four and a half yards behind him. The T's ball is in the quarterback's hands the instant it moves, and the backs, all the same depth, can hit either side of the line."
def t_formation():
    return check_legal(line5() + [
        P("LE", "TE", LINE_D, -6.2, "E"), P("RE", "TE", LINE_D, 6.2, "E"),
        P("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), P("LH", "HB", -4.6, -3.0, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0.0, "F"),
        P("RH", "HB", -4.6, 3.0, "H")])


LAT, WIN = (-10.5, 13.5), (-9.2, 2.2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.6 / 2 * (WIN[1] - WIN[0]) / (LAT[1] - LAT[0]) + 0.35))
for ax, (form, name) in zip(axes, [(single_wing(), "Single wing: direct snap"),
                                   (t_formation(), "T-formation: under center")]):
    pl = Play(form, None, los=40, to_go=None)
    pl.highlight("QB", color=BACK_RING)
    fl = pl.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=9, color=style.INK, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
    if form[0].key == "WE":
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fl, pl, 0.0, 0.0), XY(fl, pl, -4.2, 0.55)
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL,
                                     lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=5, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25"))
        label(fl, pl, "the snap flies\n5 yards", (-7.2, -6.0), target=(-2.6, 0.35), fs=6.6)
        label(fl, pl, "unbalanced:\n4 right, 2 left", (-7.4, 9.6), fs=6.6)
    else:
        label(fl, pl, "hand-to-hand snap:\nthe ball is out at once", (-7.4, -5.6), fs=6.6)
        label(fl, pl, "balanced line:\nthe same both sides", (-7.4, 9.0), fs=6.6)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.005, right=0.995, top=0.9, bottom=0.01, wspace=0.04)
plt.show()
```

The difference is all in the first second. The single wing's tailback has to catch a five-yard toss
before he can do anything; the T's quarterback has the ball the instant the center moves it, and he can
hand it to a back who is already moving toward the line.

The Chicago Bears' coach and owner, George Halas, had stuck with a version of the T through the
single-wing years, and his coach of 1930–32, Ralph Jones, is usually credited with adding a back in
[motion](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) before the snap and spreading the ends and
the backs to give it room. Clark Shaughnessy, a bookish, obsessive coach who worked with Halas as a
consultant, refined it further. In 1940 Shaughnessy installed his version at Stanford,
which had gone 1–7–1 the year before; Stanford went undefeated and won the Rose Bowl. In Chicago,
Halas had found the quarterback the system needed: Sid Luckman, a single-wing tailback at Columbia,
whom the Bears turned into a T quarterback who could take the snap, turn, fake, and drop back to
throw.[^tform40]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chicago Bears, December 8, 1940"}
Three weeks before the 1940 NFL Championship Game, Washington had beaten the Bears 7–3, and its owner,
George Preston Marshall, told reporters the Bears were "crybabies and quitters when the going got
tough." Halas pinned the articles up for his players. Shaughnessy, meanwhile, studied the game film and
saw that Washington's linebackers shifted with the Bears' man in motion, so he drew up plays that went
back the other way. On the Bears' second play from scrimmage, fullback Bill Osmanski ran 68 yards for a
touchdown. The final was **73–0**, still the most lopsided result in NFL history. The Bears scored
11 touchdowns, ten different players scored, and Chicago intercepted 8 passes. Asked whether it would
have been different if his receiver had caught a sure touchdown pass Washington dropped early in the
game, Washington's quarterback Sammy Baugh is supposed to have said: "Sure. The final score would have
been 73–7."[^tform40game]

**What to notice** (in the NFL Films highlights): how fast the backs reach the line after the snap,
and how often the play goes away from where the motion man went.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-t-counter
#| fig-cap: "The man-in-motion T and the counter that punished defenses for following the motion (an illustrative play in the style of the 1940 Bears, against a typical six-man front of the period). (1) Before the snap, the right halfback (H) starts in motion toward the sideline. (2) By the snap the linebackers (L) and the safety (S) have slid a full gap toward him. (3) The quarterback (Q) turns, the fullback (F) fakes a dive to the right, and the ball goes to the left halfback (aqua ring), who has taken a jab step right and now cuts back left. (4) The linebackers, still flowing toward the motion and the fake, are on the wrong side of the hole."
def era_six_man_balanced():
    return [D("DE_L", "DE", 1.0, -7.4, "E"), D("DT_L", "DT", 1.0, -3.8, "T"), D("DG_L", "DT", 1.2, -1.25, "G"),
            D("DG_R", "DT", 1.2, 1.25, "G"), D("DT_R", "DT", 1.0, 3.8, "T"), D("DE_R", "DE", 1.0, 7.4, "E"),
            D("LB_L", "LB", 3.8, -2.4, "L"), D("LB_R", "LB", 3.8, 2.4, "L"),
            D("HB_L", "DB", 8.0, -12.0, "H"), D("HB_R", "DB", 8.0, 12.0, "H"), D("S", "S", 13.0, 0.0, "S")]


tc = Play(t_formation(), era_six_man_balanced(), los=40, to_go=None)
tc.motion("RH", to=(-4.6, 12.5), speed=5.5)
tc.motion("LB_L", to=(3.8, 1.0), speed=2.2)                # the linebackers slide a full gap with the motion
tc.motion("LB_R", to=(3.8, 5.8), speed=2.2)
tc.motion("S", to=(13.0, 3.5), speed=2.4)
tc.motion("HB_R", to=(8.0, 14.0), speed=1.5)
# after the snap the defense chases the fake
tc.path("LB_L", [(2.6, 2.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.35, speed=3.0)
tc.path("LB_R", [(2.6, 5.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.35, speed=3.0)
tc.path("HB_L", [(6.5, -8.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.7, speed=4.0)
tc.path("S", [(9.5, -1.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.8, speed=4.5)
tc.path("QB", [(-2.7, -0.9)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
tc.path("FB", [(-3.0, 1.2), (-0.6, 2.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)          # the fake
tc.block("LT", target="DT_L", speed=2.0)
tc.block("LG", target="DG_L", speed=2.0)
tc.block("C", pts=[(1.2, 1.0)], speed=2.0)
tc.block("RG", target="DG_R", speed=2.0)
tc.block("RT", target="DT_R", speed=2.0)
tc.block("LE", target="DE_L", speed=2.0)
tc.handoff("LH", t=0.7)
tc.run("LH", [(-4.3, -2.0), (-2.8, -2.0), (-0.5, -2.4), (3.5, -2.9), (9.0, -4.2)],
       absolute=True, speed=5.5, delay=0.1)
animation_or_strip(tc, [-1.7, 0.0, 0.7, 1.8], lateral=(-15.0, 16.2), window=(-6.5, 14.8),
                   rings=[("LH", BACK_RING)], mark_r=0.85,
                   notes=["the right halfback starts\nin motion",
                          "snap: the linebackers and\nsafety have slid with him",
                          "the fullback fakes right; the\nhandoff goes back left",
                          "the counter hits where the\nlinebackers just left"])
```

The rout settled the argument. Within a decade almost every college and pro team had switched to the
T, and the Pittsburgh Steelers, the NFL's last single-wing team, gave it up after the 1952
season.[^steelers]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Halas and Shaughnessy invented the T-formation."** They didn't, and they never claimed to. A tight T
with the quarterback under center was one of football's oldest formations, and the Bears had used one
all along. What Jones, Halas and Shaughnessy built was the *modern* T: man-in-motion, wider spacing,
quick-hitting plays designed to make a defense commit, and a quarterback trained to fake and throw. The
lesson repeats through this whole part of the book: formations are rarely invented; they're
*re-equipped* for a new problem.
:::

### Why the T won

The T's advantages were speed and deception, and both came from the snap. The single wing's tailback
needed a second just to receive the ball; the T's quarterback had it instantly, and his backs could be
at the line in the time it took a single-wing snap to arrive. But the deepest reason was the
quarterback. In the single wing, the man who threw also had to run, block and often punt. In the T, one
player did nothing but handle the ball and throw it, from a few yards behind his line, *facing* his
receivers after a short drop. That made him a specialist, and specialists improve faster than
generalists. Every modern quarterback descends from Luckman more than from any single-wing tailback.

### What the T gave up, and what football did about it

The T as the Bears ran it had two tight ends and three backs: lots of runners and almost no
width. Over the next decade coaches pulled its players outward into the [pro
set](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd) of two backs, a tight end and two
wide receivers (Classic Formations has the family tree, including Shaughnessy's 1949 Rams flanking Elroy
Hirsch wide[^hirsch]). The other thing the T needed was a different kind of roster, and that required a change
in the rules.

## Platoon football: the specialist arrives

Until the 1940s the rules made substitution hard: a player who left the game generally couldn't come
back in the same quarter, so the same eleven men played offense *and* defense. The star tailback was
also a defensive back. The quarterback tackled. Linemen had to be big enough to block and quick enough
to chase.

Free substitution changed all of that. The colleges allowed it in 1941, and the NFL in 1943, both
partly because the war had thinned rosters. In 1945 Michigan's Fritz Crisler, facing a much stronger
Army team, used it to send in separate units for offense and defense, and the idea spread. The NFL made
unlimited substitution permanent in 1950. The colleges went the other way for a while: in 1953 they
went back to limited substitution, mostly over cost, because fielding two full units had pushed dozens
of small schools to drop football altogether, and they didn't restore free substitution until 1965.
That gap is part of why the pros pulled ahead in specialization.[^platoon]

The two-way player didn't vanish overnight. In 1960 injuries pushed the Philadelphia Eagles to use
Chuck Bednarik, a 12-year veteran, on both sides of the line again, at center and linebacker. In that
season's championship game he played 58 of the 60 minutes and made the game-saving tackle, wrestling
Green Bay's Jim Taylor to the ground as time ran out. He is remembered as one of the last of the NFL's
two-way stars.[^bednarik]

That is [**platoon football**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-platoon-football): separate groups of
players for offense and defense, and eventually for kicking plays and particular situations.

### Why it mattered

Platooning sounds like a roster rule. It was really a revolution in what a player could be.

- **Bodies could specialize.** An offensive lineman no longer needed to chase a halfback; he could get
  bigger and stronger and learn to pass block. A defensive back no longer needed to run the ball; he
  could be the fastest man on the field and learn to cover.
- **Skills could specialize.** A T quarterback could spend his whole practice throwing. A defensive
  end could spend his rushing. The pass-catching end became a receiver who ran routes for a living.
- **Coaching could specialize.** Two units meant two sets of schemes, and soon two sets of coaches:
  the ancestors of today's [offensive and defensive
  coordinators](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd).

Everything after this point in the chapter is an argument between specialists.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In *Madden* you never think about who plays defense when your offense is on the field: there are 53
players and the game substitutes for you. For football's first half-century that roster didn't exist.
NFL roster limits ran from about 20 players in the early 1930s to the low and mid-30s in the '40s, and
the best players stayed on the field for both halves of every possession.[^rosters] The
whole modern idea of *personnel groupings* (Part 2) depends on free substitution. Before 1943 there were
no groupings to choose between: to borrow the phrase in a different sense, a team's "11 personnel" was
simply its eleven best players, and they were the defense too.
:::

## Paul Brown: football becomes a profession

The coach who did the most with those specialists was Paul Brown. He had built winners at Massillon
(Ohio) High School and at Ohio State, where his 1942 team won the national championship, and in 1946 he
became head coach of a new professional team named after him, the Cleveland Browns of the
All-America Football Conference (AAFC), a rival league. The Browns won all four AAFC championships
(1946–49). When the AAFC folded and the Browns joined the NFL in 1950, the established league assumed
they would be humbled. In their first NFL game, against the two-time defending champion Philadelphia
Eagles, the Browns won 35–10. They won the NFL title that season and again in 1954 and 1955, and they
played in the championship game in each of their first ten seasons (AAFC and NFL) with Otto Graham at
quarterback.[^brown]

Brown's innovations matter more than his trophies, because almost all of them are still standard:

- **A full-time, year-round coaching staff**, at a time when many assistants were part-timers.
- **The playbook as a textbook.** Players got detailed books of formations and plays, attended
  classroom sessions, and took written tests on them. Brown also gave them intelligence tests.
- **Film study.** Brown is credited with being the first coach to use game film to scout opponents,
  breaking down what the other team did before playing it.
- **Measurable athletes.** He timed players over 40 yards, a distance he adopted at Ohio State in
  1941, by the usual account because it was about how far a player ran on a punt cover (his son Mike
  remembers it as simply the longest sprint a player usually had to make). The 40-yard dash is still the most
  famous number at the NFL Combine.
- **The draw play**, which Brown dated to an accident in 1946: Otto Graham, about to be sacked,
  handed the ball to his fullback, Marion Motley, who ran through a defense that had dropped back for
  a pass. (A [draw play](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) is a run disguised as a pass:
  the linemen show pass protection, then the ball goes to a back.)
- **Integration.** In 1946 Brown signed Motley and guard Bill Willis, two of the first Black players
  in modern pro football.

### The coach calls the plays

The innovation that changed the game most directly was who called the plays. Before Brown, the
quarterback called them in the huddle. Brown called them from the sideline, and to get his calls in,
he rotated two guards on every play: each **messenger guard** came in with the call and the other went
out. Guards were the natural men to shuttle. Two guards of similar size and skill could swap every play
without changing what the offense could do, whereas swapping a back or a receiver would have changed
the personnel on the field, and the quarterback had to stay in to run the play. One of them, from 1953 to 1959, was a smart, undersized lineman named Chuck Noll, who, Brown
said, soon could have called the plays himself; Noll later coached the 1970s Steelers. In 1956 Brown
went further and tested a radio receiver in his quarterback's helmet. The Detroit Lions spotted the
transmitter during a preseason game, and Commissioner Bert Bell banned the device after a handful of
games. The NFL legalized helmet radios in 1994.[^radio]

A coach choosing every play from the sideline is so normal now (see [What a Play Really
Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)) that it's easy to miss how radical it was. It
moved the brain of the offense from the field to the staff, and it made the game plan, built from
film during the week, the center of football. Every coordinator with a laminated [call
sheet](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) works in a system Paul Brown designed.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cleveland Browns vs. Philadelphia Eagles, 1950"}
The Browns' first NFL game, on September 16, 1950, was the AAFC champion against the NFL champion,
and Otto Graham passed for 346 yards and three touchdowns in a 35–10 win. The Eagles' coach, Greasy
Neale, whose five-man [Eagle defense](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)
had won the previous two NFL titles, grumbled that the Browns were like a basketball team, all they did
was throw. When the teams met again on December 3, in rain in Cleveland, Brown answered him: the
Browns won 13–7 **without a single official pass attempt**. (The two passes Graham threw were both
called back by penalties.) No NFL team since has played a whole game without attempting a
pass.[^eagles50]

**What to notice:** the point Brown was making. A team whose opponent can only stop one thing doesn't
have to do only one thing. The pass had become a weapon because it was no longer the *only* weapon.
:::

## The defense answers: Steve Owen's umbrella

First, what had the defense done about the T? Through the 1940s, most teams' answer was more men on the
line and more men deep. The most successful version was Greasy Neale's **Eagle defense** in
Philadelphia, a 5-2-4 from 1947: five linemen, with a *middle guard* head-up on the center, two
linebackers behind them, and four defensive backs instead of the three of the single-wing era, the
extra one for the T's passes. The Eagles won the 1948 and 1949 titles with it.
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) follows
the five-man line from there to the 3-4. Its soft spot was the middle: with no linebacker over the
center, a quick pass over the middle guard's head had room.[^eagle47] Keep that in mind; it comes back
in a few pages.

Brown's passing game created a problem defenses of 1950 had never had to solve. Most NFL teams still
lined up with five or six linemen and only three or four defensive backs, and the Browns sent out
receivers like Dante Lavelli and Mac Speedie, plus a flanker, plus backs who ran routes. There were
more receivers than defenders who could cover them.

The first team to solve it was the New York Giants. Their head coach, Steve Owen, a heavyset Oklahoman
who had been coaching the Giants since 1930 and had won the NFL title in 1934 and 1938, built a defense
for the 1950 Browns that looked like a run defense and played like a pass defense. Owen called it a
6-1-4, and in his own words, on many plays it became "a 4-1-6 in reality." The secret was the two
defensive ends: they lined up on the line of scrimmage like linemen, and at the snap they could drop
back into pass coverage. The four defensive backs behind them, spread in an arc like the ribs of an
umbrella, gave the defense its name: the [**umbrella
defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-umbrella-defense). One of those defensive backs, a young
Texan named Tom Landry, explained it to the others and taught it on the field.[^owen]

```{python}
#| label: fig-umbrella
#| fig-cap: "Owen's umbrella against a Browns-style pass (an illustrative reconstruction: the Browns' formation and routes varied). (1) Before the snap the Giants show a 6-1-4: six men on the line, one linebacker (M) and four defensive backs (two halfbacks H, two safeties S) in an arc, the umbrella. The two ends (E, orange rings) stand at the ends of the line. (2–3) At the snap the ends drop into the short outside zones (the flats), the linebacker drops to the middle, and the halfbacks and safeties retreat, the halfbacks staying shallower and wider so the arc keeps its umbrella shape. (4) Against the pass it is now a 4-1-6: four rushers and seven defenders in coverage, more than the five receivers the offense can send. Against a run, those same two ends are the defense's edge (contain) players, which is the umbrella's trade: an end who drops on a run has left the edge open. Offense: Q quarterback, F fullback, H halfback, X and Y split ends, Z flanker."
def browns_t():
    return check_legal(line5() + [
        P("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0.0, "F"), P("HB", "HB", -4.6, 2.4, "H"),
        P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 9.6, "Y"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)])


def umbrella_def():
    return [D("dLE", "DE", 1.0, -6.4, "E"), D("dLT", "DT", 1.0, -3.4, "T"), D("dLG", "DT", 1.0, -1.0, "G"),
            D("dRG", "DT", 1.0, 1.0, "G"), D("dRT", "DT", 1.0, 3.4, "T"), D("dRE", "DE", 1.0, 6.4, "E"),
            D("M", "MIKE", 4.0, 0.0, "M"),
            D("LH", "DB", 7.0, -12.5, "H"), D("RH", "DB", 7.0, 13.5, "H"),
            D("LS", "S", 11.5, -5.0, "S"), D("RS", "S", 11.5, 5.5, "S")]


um = Play(browns_t(), umbrella_def(), los=35, to_go=None)
um.dropback(5.0)
um.route("X", [(0, 0), (12.0, 0), (10.8, -1.5)])        # curl
um.route("Y", [(0, 0), (11.0, 0), (11.0, 5.0)])         # sideline out
um.route("Z", [(0, 0), (15.0, -0.5)])                   # go
um.route("HB", [(0, 0), (-0.6, 3.5), (1.5, 8.0)], side=1)  # swing to the flat
um.block("FB", pts=[(0.6, -1.5)], speed=2.0)
um.drop("dLE", (6.5, -11.0), delay=0.1)
um.drop("dRE", (6.0, 12.4), delay=0.3)
um.drop("M", (8.5, 0.5), delay=0.15)
um.drop("LH", (13.5, -13.6), delay=0.1)
um.drop("RH", (13.6, 12.0), delay=0.1)
um.drop("LS", (16.8, -5.0), delay=0.1)
um.drop("RS", (16.8, 5.5), delay=0.1)
for k in ("dLT", "dLG", "dRG", "dRT"):            # four rush and meet the blockers
    um.path(k, [(-0.1, um.players[k].w)], absolute=True, speed=1.5)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    um.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
animation_or_strip(um, [0.0, 0.7, 1.4, 2.2], lateral=(-15.0, 17.0), window=(-8.5, 19.5),
                   rings=[("dLE", KEY_RING), ("dRE", KEY_RING)], mark_r=0.9,
                   notes=["snap: a 6-1-4, six men\non the line",
                          "the two ends turn and drop",
                          "the ends reach the flats;\nthe umbrella opens",
                          "a 4-1-6: four rush,\nseven cover"])
```

It worked. On October 1, 1950, the Giants beat the Browns 6–0, the first time Cleveland had ever been
shut out, and they beat them again, 17–13, later in the season. Cleveland lost only those two games
and then beat the Giants 8–3 in a playoff on the way to the title, but the umbrella had shown what
mattered: **a defense that can change its shape after the snap can show one thing and play another.**
That's the seed of every disguise in [Part 6](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).

The trade, as always, was real. An umbrella end who dropped into coverage on a run play was out of
position, and on a pass the defense rushed only four men instead of the six the era was used to. Against a team with a dangerous runner who
could hit a draw (Brown had Motley), dropping the ends could be expensive.

### From the umbrella to the 4-3

The 4-3 came from two different parents, each of which gave up a lineman.

The first parent is the umbrella. Its dropping ends were really linebackers who started on the line.
Stand them up for good and the 6-1-4 becomes four linemen, three linebackers (the two ends and the one
linebacker) and four defensive backs.

The second parent is the five-man front of the Eagle family. Its weak spot, you'll remember, was the
middle. In 1954 the Bears' middle guard, Bill George, kept getting beaten by quick passes thrown over
his head, so he started standing up and backing off the line at the snap. Do that in a 5-2-4 and it
becomes four linemen, three linebackers (the two and George) and four defensive backs. George is
usually named as the first true middle linebacker, though the Hall of Fame itself says no one can be
sure which middle guard first dropped back.[^george]

```{python}
#| label: fig-43-parents
#| fig-cap: "Two roads to the 4-3 (a schematic, not to scale; each row is a level of the defense: linemen, linebackers, defensive backs). Left, Owen's 6-1-4 umbrella: stand its two ends up (orange rings) and they become outside linebackers. Right, the 5-2-4 Eagle-style front: stand the middle guard up (orange ring) and he becomes the middle linebacker. Both arrive at the same place, in the middle: four linemen, three linebackers, four defensive backs."
def tier(ax, x0, rows, moved=(), title=""):
    """rows: counts per level (DL, LB, DB); moved: (row, index) pairs to ring."""
    ys = [0.0, -1.0, -2.0]
    for r, (n, y) in enumerate(zip(rows, ys)):
        xs = [x0 + (i - (n - 1) / 2) * 0.55 for i in range(n)]
        for i, x in enumerate(xs):
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=0.2, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                                        ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
            if (r, i) in moved:
                ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.27, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, zorder=4))
    ax.text(x0, 0.75, title, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    ax.text(x0, -2.75, "-".join(str(n) for n in rows), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.0, color=style.INK_2)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.1))
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 12.2); ax.set_ylim(-3.1, 1.1); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
tier(ax, 1.85, (6, 1, 4), moved={(0, 0), (0, 5)}, title="Umbrella (1950)")
tier(ax, 6.0, (4, 3, 4), title="4-3 (Landry, 1956)")
tier(ax, 10.15, (5, 2, 4), moved={(0, 2)}, title="Eagle-style 5-2-4")
for xa, xb, txt in [(3.75, 4.85, "ends\nstand up"), (8.65, 7.15, "middle guard\nstands up")]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xa, -1.0), (xb, -1.0), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11,
                                 color=style.INK_2, lw=1.2))
    ax.text((xa + xb) / 2, -0.45, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

Landry took both moves at once: the umbrella's idea of ends who could play off the line became his
outside linebackers, and George's stand-up middle guard became his middle linebacker. Four linemen,
three linebackers and four defensive backs: the [4-3](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd).
Landry, by then the Giants' defensive coach, made it the Giants' base defense in 1956, built around a
rookie middle linebacker from West Virginia, Sam Huff. The Giants won the 1956 championship, much of
the league copied the defense the following season, and Huff became so famous that CBS made a
television documentary about him, *The Violent World of Sam
Huff* (1960, an episode of Walter Cronkite's *The Twentieth Century*). The
4-3 would be the NFL's standard defense for the next two decades.[^landry43] [A First Look at
Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) and [Even
Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd) cover how it lines up today.

Why did the 4-3 win? Because it was the first defense balanced for *both* threats. Four linemen are
enough to rush a passer; three linebackers can stop a run or drop into coverage; four defensive backs
can cover the receivers that platoon football had produced. It was the defense equivalent of the pro
set: good at everything, great at nothing in particular.

## Lombardi's sweep and Landry's Flex

### The offense: run to daylight

Vince Lombardi arrived in Green Bay in 1959 as a 45-year-old assistant who had never been a head coach
in the NFL. (He had been the Giants' offensive coach, across the hall from Landry, in the 1950s.) His
Packers won five NFL championships in seven seasons, 1961–67, including the first two Super Bowls, and
the play everyone associated with them was the **power sweep**. [Gap and Power
Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) draws it block by block; here is the version
that matters for the history.

```{python}
#| label: fig-power-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Lombardi's power sweep to the right from split backs (an illustrative reconstruction against a 1960s 4-3; landmarks varied). Both guards (G, dark rings) pull: the right guard to the first defender outside (here the cornerback), the left guard turning up inside for the pursuit (the Mike). The fullback (F) blocks the defensive end, the tight end (Y) takes the Sam linebacker (S), and the flanker (Z) blocks the strong safety. The halfback (H, aqua ring) takes the handoff, presses the edge about a yard outside the tight end and reads the block on the Sam there: if the Sam is driven outside, he cuts inside it; if the Sam fights inside, he runs around it. That choice is 'running to daylight.'"
def pro_set_red():
    """Split backs set wide apart (Lombardi's 'Red'), tight end and flanker to the right."""
    return check_legal(line5() + [
        P("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), P("HB", "HB", -5.0, -2.8, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.8, "F"),
        P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W, "Y"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.0)])


def base43_60s(fix=None):
    d = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
         D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.2, "E"), D("SAM", "SAM", 3.6, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.3, 0.6, "M"),
         D("WILL", "WILL", 4.3, -3.2, "W"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.0, "C"),
         D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -6.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 7.5, "SS")]
    fix = fix or {}
    return [q.moved(**fix[q.key]) if q.key in fix else q for q in d]


sweep_off = [OL(q.key, q.w, "G") if q.key in ("LG", "RG") else q for q in pro_set_red()]
sweep = Play(sweep_off, base43_60s(), los=35, to_go=None)
sweep.path("MIKE", [(3.4, 4.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.4, speed=3.5)
sweep.block("Y", target="SAM")
sweep.block("RT", target="SDT")
sweep.block("C", target="WDT")
sweep.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)])
sweep.block("FB", target="SDE", speed=4.0)
sweep.pull("RG", [(-0.6, 0.6), (-0.7, 5.9), (2.2, 8.4), (6.0, 9.4)], speed=5.0)     # onside guard: the corner
sweep.pull("LG", [(-1.5, 1.2), (-1.6, 6.6), (1.6, 7.2), (3.8, 5.3)], speed=5.0)     # offside guard: up inside
sweep.block("Z", target="SS", speed=3.0)
sweep.path("QB", [(-2.7, -1.1), (-3.2, -1.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
sweep.handoff("HB", t=0.8)
sweep.run("HB", [(-5.1, -0.6), (-6.0, 2.4), (-4.0, 5.3), (-0.6, 6.4)], absolute=True, speed=6.2)
sweep.highlight("HB", color=BACK_RING)
sweep.highlight("LG", "RG", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw_play(sweep, lateral=(-16.5, 19.0), window=(-8.0, 15.5))
dashed_arrow(fld, sweep, [(-0.6, 6.4), (2.8, 6.0), (6.4, 5.4)])
dashed_arrow(fld, sweep, [(-0.6, 6.4), (2.6, 8.6), (6.2, 11.8)])
label(fld, sweep, "daylight: inside\nthe Sam", (8.6, 3.6), color=THREAT)
label(fld, sweep, "or outside\nhim", (8.9, 14.6), color=THREAT)
label(fld, sweep, "right guard: kicks out\nor logs the corner", (13.0, 13.4), target=(5.3, 9.3))
label(fld, sweep, "left guard: turns up\ninside, on the Mike", (9.0, -9.0), target=(3.7, 4.4))
label(fld, sweep, "the halfback reads\nthe Sam's block here", (-6.4, 11.4), target=(-0.6, 6.4))
label(fld, sweep, "split backs, set wide", (-6.6, -7.0))
plt.show()
```

The sweep's genius was that it didn't need to fool anyone. Lombardi drilled it until every block was
automatic, and the runner was given a lane, not a hole. A *hole* is a fixed spot the play is designed
to hit ("between the guard and the tackle"), and the back runs there whatever happens. A *lane* is
wherever the defense isn't once the blocks are made: the blockers take defenders the way they want to
go, and the back finds the opening the blocks create. Lombardi's own phrase for it, and the title of his
1963 book, was *run to daylight*. The defense knew the sweep was coming, and the Packers ran it anyway.

Underneath the sweep was a blocking idea that defenses found maddening, which coaches of the era called
*option blocking* (not to be confused with the [option
offense](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd), where the *quarterback* reads a defender). Here
the blocker has the choice. Say the tight end's job is the Sam linebacker. If the Sam steps outside,
the tight end doesn't fight to move him back in; he rides him farther outside, and the runner cuts
inside. If the Sam steps inside, the tight end seals him there, and the runner goes around. Block the man
where he goes, not to a spot, and let the runner read the result. The pulling guards read the same
block: the right guard logs the cornerback inside or kicks him out, depending on which side of him he
can reach, and the left guard turns up through whichever seam the tight end's block has opened. A
defense built on linemen charging hard into the backfield, each guessing his own way, helped option
blocking. The harder a lineman charged, the easier he was to push past the hole, and the daylight
appeared behind him.

### The answer: the Flex

Tom Landry left the Giants to become the first head coach of the expansion Dallas Cowboys in 1960. His
problem, as the Cowboys grew into contenders, was Green Bay. His answer, developed in the mid-1960s
(sources date its first use anywhere from 1964 to 1966), was the [**Flex
defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flex-defense).[^flex]

```{python}
#| label: fig-flex
#| fig-cap: "Landry's Flex against the same split-backs formation (illustrative; which two linemen flexed changed with the formation and with what Dallas expected the offense to do; zoomed on the box, so the wide receivers are out of the picture). Two of the four defensive linemen (orange rings) line up about a yard off the ball, where they can read the blocks before they move; the other two stay on the line and charge into their gaps. The shaded lanes are the gaps between blockers (A next to the center, then B, C and D outward), and each lane has one defender standing in it: the ends (E) in the C gaps, the tackles (T) and the Mike (M) in the A and B gaps, the Will (W) in the weak-side B gap and the Sam (S) outside the tight end. A runner looking for daylight finds a defender already in every lane. Offense: Q quarterback, H halfback, F fullback, Y tight end."
flex_fix = {"SDE": dict(d=2.2, w=4.2), "WDT": dict(d=2.2, w=-0.9), "SDT": dict(w=2.4), "WDE": dict(w=-4.0),
            "SAM": dict(d=3.4, w=5.7), "MIKE": dict(d=4.6, w=0.8), "WILL": dict(d=4.6, w=-2.4)}
box_off = [q for q in pro_set_red() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")]               # zoomed on the box
box_def = [q for q in base43_60s(flex_fix) if q.key not in ("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")]
fx = Play(box_off, box_def, los=35, to_go=None)
fx.highlight("SDE", "WDT", color=KEY_RING)
fld = draw_play(fx, lateral=(-10.5, 10.5), window=(-6.6, 10.6))
LANES = [("C", -4.8, -3.2), ("B", -3.2, -1.6), ("A", -1.6, 0.0), ("A", 0.0, 1.6), ("B", 1.6, 3.2),
         ("C", 3.2, TE_W), ("D", TE_W, TE_W + 1.6)]
for i, (g, w0, w1) in enumerate(LANES):
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = XY(fld, fx, 0.15, w0), XY(fld, fx, 5.7, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(xa, xb), min(ya, yb)), abs(xb - xa), abs(yb - ya),
                               fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.06 if i % 2 else 0.13, ec="none", zorder=0.6))
    x, y = XY(fld, fx, 6.35, (w0 + w1) / 2)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, g, fontsize=8.5, ha="center", va="center", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold",
                zorder=9)
label(fld, fx, "seven lanes (gaps), seven owners", (8.0, 0.0))
label(fld, fx, "flexed: a yard off the ball,\nreads the blocks, then fills", (8.5, -6.4), target=(2.2, -0.9))
label(fld, fx, "flexed end: reads the\ntackle and tight end", (8.5, 6.6), target=(2.2, 4.2))
label(fld, fx, "on the ball: charges\ninto his gap", (-3.8, -7.4), target=(1.0, -4.0))
plt.show()
```

In the Flex, two of the four defensive linemen line up about a yard off the ball while the other two
stay on the line. The flexed linemen are in no hurry to charge: they read the blocks in front of them,
then step into the gap they're assigned. The linemen on the line attack their gaps. Linebackers fill the
rest. The result is a defense in which **every gap has an owner who is already standing in it** before
the runner arrives, which is exactly what run-to-daylight blocking can't handle: there is no daylight to
run to.

Why does a single yard matter so much? Think about it from the blocker's side. Option blocking works on
a defender who is already moving: you take his momentum and add to it. A flexed lineman isn't moving.
The yard of space means the blocker has to travel to reach him, which takes a moment, and in that moment
the defender sees where the block is coming from. And because he hasn't committed to a direction, there
is no momentum for the blocker to use. A blocker trying to push a flexed defender "the way he wants to
go" finds that he doesn't want to go anywhere until he knows where the ball is.

But the two linemen on the ball do charge, so why weren't *they* option-blocked? Because their charge
is into an assigned gap, not a free-lance guess at where the play is going. A tackle who knows he owns
the A gap gets there and holds it; if he is pushed past it, the flexed man behind him is reading that
very block and steps into the space he left. The on-ball men, in other words, are there to occupy
blockers and keep their own gaps, and the flexed men clean up behind them. Landry built it partly around
the quickness of his great defensive tackle, Bob Lilly, who could play on the ball and get into his gap
before a blocker touched him.

Why flex only two, and not all four? Because somebody still has to take on the blockers at the snap and
threaten the quarterback. A line with all four men standing a yard off the ball reading would give the
offense a free first step everywhere and no pass rush at all. Which two flexed changed with the
offense's formation and with where Dallas expected the run.

The Flex was Landry's style in one picture: precise, rule-bound, analytical. Players learned exactly
which step to take with which foot, which some of them hated. Its price was the pass rush *from the
Flex itself*: linemen standing back reading blocks aren't rushing the quarterback. So Dallas used it as
a run-down defense, almost always on first down but mostly only in running situations on second and
third, and on clear passing downs the linemen lined up on the ball and rushed. They could rush, too: the
Cowboys' defense of the 1970s, nicknamed the **Doomsday Defense**, had Harvey Martin, credited
unofficially with 23 sacks in 1977.[^flexrush] Dallas reached two straight NFL Championship Games
against Green Bay, and later won Super Bowls after the 1971 and 1977 seasons with the Flex behind them.
You have met its descendant: the idea that every defender owns a gap is the core of [gap
integrity and run fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Green Bay Packers vs. Dallas Cowboys, December 31, 1967"}
The 1967 NFL Championship Game, the "Ice Bowl," was played in Green Bay in a temperature of about
−13°F. It was Lombardi's offense against Landry's Flex for the second year in a row (Green Bay had won
the 1966 title game 34–27). Trailing 17–14 late in the fourth quarter, the Packers drove the length of
the field. The play that got them to the goal line was built to beat the Flex. On a call the Packers
named 54-Give, which Lombardi called the "sucker" play, left guard Gale Gillingham pulled to his right as
if it were the sweep. Bob Lilly, taught to read the guard in front of him and follow him, did exactly
that, and fullback Chuck Mercein ran straight through the space Lilly had left, from the Dallas 11 to
the 3. Then, with seconds left and the ball inside the 1-yard line, Bart Starr conferred with Lombardi
and kept the ball on a quarterback sneak: he followed guard Jerry Kramer's block (a double-team with
center Ken Bowman) on Dallas tackle Jethro Pugh and scored with 13 seconds left. Green Bay won 21–17
and went on to win Super Bowl II.[^icebowl]

**What to notice** (NFL Films' footage is everywhere): Mercein's run. A defense that reads and follows
blocks can be led away by a block that lies, which is the counterpunch to every read-and-react
defense: an *influence* or "sucker" play. You'll also notice how rarely either team breaks a long run;
the frozen field explains as much of that as the Flex does.
:::

## Sid Gillman and the vertical passing game

While Lombardi and Landry argued about the run, Sid Gillman was building the passing game you watch
today. As a young man in Minneapolis, Gillman worked in his family's movie theater and cut the football
clips out of the newsreels so he could study them at home on a projector. He became the coach most
associated with film study, and he used it to take passing apart. He coached the Los Angeles Rams
(1955–59) and then the Chargers of the new AFL (1960–69), who won the 1963 AFL championship 51–10 over
Boston.[^gillman]

Gillman's idea, in one sentence: **use all of the field, deep and wide, so that the defense can't
protect all of it.** Defenses of the 1950s and early '60s were happy to let an offense throw short in
front of them, and for a good reason: a short completion was a few yards and a tackle. To score that way
an offense had to string together a long series of plays without an incompletion on a key down, a
penalty or an interception (and interceptions were far more common then than now), so the defense's
first job was to stop the long ball and wait for the drive to die. Gillman threw deep first, with fast
receivers like Lance Alworth, to push the safeties back, and then attacked the room that left
underneath: intermediate routes, and backs released into the flats. As Al Davis, who coached under him,
put it, people thought of the passing game as vertical, the length of the field, "but Sid also thought
of it as horizontal."

The mechanism under the slogan was timing. Gillman tied each route to the quarterback's drop: on a
five-step drop, the first receiver's route was built to break just as the quarterback finished his
last step, so the ball could leave before the receiver turned around, and the next receiver's route came
open a beat later for the next read.[^gillmantiming] A defense can't cover a throw that arrives before
it has seen the receiver's break. That idea, routes and drops on one clock, is what Don Coryell and Bill
Walsh inherited.

He was building it, mostly, against man-to-man coverage. Much of the era's pass defense, and especially
the AFL's, was man-to-man with a free safety behind it; the AFL is where the *bump-and-run*, a cornerback
pressing his receiver and jamming him at the line, took hold in the 1960s, with Oakland's Willie Brown
its best-known practitioner. Beating man coverage is about getting one receiver open against one
defender, and the whole-field spacing gave Gillman's receivers room to do it. Remember that when you
reach the 1970s: the defenses' answer to the passing decade was to stop playing man and play zones as a
team.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gillman
#| fig-cap: "Gillman's principle with his AFL Chargers: stretch the defense deep and wide at once (an illustrative pass from split backs against a 1960s 4-3 with two safeties deep, not a specific Chargers play). The flanker's go route (Z) runs at the deep safety (SS) and drives him back; the split end's comeback (X) and the tight end's dig (Y) settle in the intermediate band the safeties have just left (the dashed squares show where the safeties finish); the halfback and fullback release to the flats, so the linebackers have someone short to worry about on both sides. Three depths and the full width, on every pass: the defense can't be everywhere."
gl = Play(pro_set_red(), base43_60s({"FS": dict(d=12.0, w=-8.0)}), los=30, to_go=None)
gl.dropback(7.0)
gl.route("Z", [(0, 0), (6.0, 0.4), (27.0, 1.6)])
gl.route("X", [(0, 0), (16.0, 0), (14.0, 2.8)])
gl.route("Y", [(0, 0), (13.0, 0), (13.0, -8.4)])
gl.route("HB", [(0, 0), (2.0, 3.4), (8.0, 9.7)], side=-1)
gl.route("FB", [(0, 0), (2.0, 3.0), (8.0, 6.7)], side=1)
gl.drop("SS", (21.0, 9.5), delay=0.2)
gl.drop("FS", (20.0, -7.5), delay=0.2)
gl.drop("RCB", (17.0, 14.0), delay=0.2)
gl.drop("LCB", (12.0, -15.0), delay=0.2)
gl.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 0.5), delay=0.3)
gl.drop("SAM", (8.0, 7.5), delay=0.3)
gl.drop("WILL", (8.0, -6.5), delay=0.3)
fld = draw_play(gl, lateral=(-24.5, 19.5), window=(-9.5, 31.0))
for (lo, hi, name) in [(18.0, 30.0, "deep"), (9.5, 17.5, "intermediate"), (-1.0, 6.5, "short")]:
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = XY(fld, gl, lo, -24.5), XY(fld, gl, hi, 19.5)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(xa, xb), min(ya, yb)), abs(xb - xa), abs(yb - ya), fc=style.OFFENSE,
                               alpha=0.05, ec="none", zorder=0.5))
    label(fld, gl, name, ((lo + hi) / 2, -21.0), fs=7.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
label(fld, gl, "the go route pushes\nthe safety deep", (27.0, 4.2), target=(21.0, 9.5))
label(fld, gl, "the flats: backs\non both sides", (-6.6, -15.6), target=(2.4, -12.0))
for key, (d, w) in {"FS": (20.0, -7.5), "SS": (21.0, 9.5)}.items():      # where the safeties finish
    x, y = XY(fld, gl, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=1.05, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), alpha=0.75, zorder=7))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, key, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2, fontweight="bold", zorder=8)
plt.show()
```

Gillman's coaching descendants are a who's who of the next chapter: Al Davis (whose Raiders threw deep
for thirty years), Chuck Noll, Bill Walsh (who coached under Davis in Oakland) and Dick Vermeil, and Don
Coryell studied him closely. When you meet [Air Coryell](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd)
and the [West Coast offense](../12-case-studies/12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd), you are meeting
Gillman's grandchildren. The [vertical and horizontal
stretches](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) of Part 4 are his vocabulary.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Diego Chargers, 1963 AFL Championship Game"}
On January 5, 1964, Gillman's Chargers beat the Boston Patriots 51–10 in San Diego. The star was
halfback Keith Lincoln, who ran for 206 yards on 13 carries and led the team with 123 receiving yards,
the kind of two-way threat out of the backfield that Gillman's spread-the-field passing game created
room for.[^chargers63]

**What to notice:** how wide the Chargers' receivers and backs spread the Patriots, and how many of the
big plays come from backs running routes against linebackers.
:::

## The AFL: a passing laboratory

In August 1959 a young Texan named Lamar Hunt, who had been refused an NFL expansion team, founded
a league of his own. The [**AFL**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-afl) ([**American Football
League**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-american-football-league)) began play in 1960 with eight
teams, and it needed fans, so it needed points.

The AFL was looser in almost every way. It added the **two-point conversion** (the NFL would not adopt
it until 1994), put players' names on their jerseys (a habit the NFL later copied), and shared its
television money equally, including, from 1965, a five-year NBC contract worth \$36 million that kept
the league alive. Because it
was scrambling for talent, it took players the NFL had overlooked: quarterbacks cut by NFL teams,
small-college stars, and many players from historically Black colleges that NFL scouts had largely
ignored.[^afl]

Why call it a *passing* laboratory? Because its best offenses built their identity on throwing deep to
wide receivers. Gillman's Chargers, the
plate above, were the model: Alworth deep, the tight end and the backs underneath, every throw timed to
the drop. Al Davis took the same idea to Oakland in 1963 and made the deep ball the Raiders' trademark
for decades: stretch the field vertically and use every eligible receiver.[^davis] Quarterbacks like John Hadl,
Len Dawson and Daryle Lamonica threw deep and often. The points chart below shows the result: in each of
its first five seasons AFL teams outscored NFL teams, by close to three points a game in 1960 and 1961,
and by about one point a game in 1962–64. And the AFL's defenses answered in kind, with the
bump-and-run corners you met above. The arms race of the next decade was rehearsed here.

### Hank Stram's Chiefs

The most inventive AFL coach after Gillman was Hank Stram, who led the Dallas Texans and then the Kansas
City Chiefs from 1960 to 1974 and won three AFL titles (1962, 1966 and 1969). Stram's contributions to
the passing game and to everything around it:

- **The moving pocket.** The protection shifted with a quarterback who set up somewhere other than
  straight behind the center, so the rushers had a moving target and the quarterback got a clear
  throwing lane. Part 4's [bootlegs and sprint-outs](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
  are its heirs.
- **New formations.** He is credited with being the first pro coach to use both the I-formation and the
  two-tight-end offense.
- **The triple stack on defense.** Linebackers hid directly behind defensive linemen, so the offense
  couldn't tell which gap each would attack.
- **Talent from where others weren't looking.** He drafted heavily from historically Black colleges:
  defensive tackle Buck Buchanan (Grambling) and linebacker Willie Lanier (Morgan State) are both in the
  Hall of Fame.

In Super Bowl IV Stram wore a microphone for NFL Films, usually described as a first for a pro coach, and
it caught him gleefully telling his team to keep "matriculating the ball down the field," and the Chiefs
beat Minnesota 23–7.[^stram]

### The merger

The two leagues spent the early 1960s bidding against each other for players, and when the Jets signed
Alabama quarterback Joe Namath on January 2, 1965, for a reported \$427,000, the NFL owners decided the
war was too expensive. The leagues announced a merger on June 8, 1966: a common draft, a championship
game between them (the first, in January 1967, became known as Super Bowl I), and a single league from
1970. The NFL's champions won the first two Super Bowls easily. Then the AFL won the next two: Namath's
