Jets beat the Baltimore Colts 16–7 in Super Bowl III, and Stram's Chiefs beat the Vikings in Super Bowl
IV. When the merger took effect in 1970, the AFL's ten teams (eight originals plus two later additions,
Miami in 1966 and Cincinnati in 1968) and three NFL teams (the Colts, Browns and Steelers) formed the
American Football Conference.

The AFL's lasting gift was proof. Wide-open passing offenses could win championships, not just
entertain, and the merged league inherited the coaches, quarterbacks and ideas to play that way. That
makes what happened next all the stranger.

### Meanwhile in the NFL: the 1960 shotgun

The NFL had its own experiment. On November 27, 1960, San Francisco's coach, Red Hickey, lined his
quarterback up about seven yards behind the center, a long direct snap away, with the backs and
receivers spread around him. It was "really just a new version of an old formation," the single wing's
direct snap with a passer instead of a runner, and Hickey called it the *shotgun*. As a heavy underdog
the 49ers upset the Colts 30–22. In 1961 Hickey rotated three quarterbacks (John Brodie, Billy Kilmer
and Bobby Waters) through it and started 4–1, including 49–0 over Detroit and 35–0 over the Rams. On
October 22, 1961, the Bears found an answer, beat San Francisco 31–0, and Hickey shelved the
formation.[^shotgun] (What the Bears did is the second Predict-the-play drill below; try it before you
look it up.) The shotgun returned in Dallas in 1975 as a passing-down weapon, and [Formation
Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) tells the rest; today's
NFL offenses spend most of their snaps in it.

## The 1970s scoring drought

Now the chart. It shows how many points the average NFL team scored per game, every season from 1932
to 1977, with the AFL's teams drawn separately for the 1960s.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ppg
#| fig-cap: "Points per team per game, regular season, 1932–1977. NFL (blue) and, for its ten seasons, the AFL (orange). Scoring nearly tripled between 1932 and 1948 as the passing rules loosened and the T arrived, held near 21–22 through the 1950s and '60s, and then fell through the 1970s (shaded) to 17.2 in 1977, the lowest since 1942, despite rule changes in 1972, 1974 and 1977 (marked) meant to raise it. Computed from every game's final score (AAFC games of 1946–49 excluded; course calculation, see the note)."
URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/nfl-elo-game/master/data/nfl_games.csv"
AFL_TEAMS = {"BUF", "DEN", "KC", "LAC", "OAK", "NE", "NYJ", "TEN", "MIA", "CIN"}     # franchise codes, 1960-69
AAFC_TEAMS = {"BBA", "BDA", "CLE", "CRA", "LDA", "MSA", "NAA", "SF", "BCL"}         # 1946-49 only
FALLBACK = {  # the same calculation, stored in case the source file can't be fetched
    "NFL": [8.21, 9.69, 10.75, 10.92, 11.89, 12.95, 13.49, 15.38, 15.06, 16.47, 15.86, 19.45, 18.01, 18.49,
            18.90, 21.95, 23.24, 22.49, 22.94, 21.94, 22.28, 21.51, 21.89, 20.84, 20.38, 19.79, 22.59, 21.33,
            21.56, 21.51, 22.31, 21.98, 22.04, 23.06, 21.72, 21.85, 20.50, 20.90, 19.26, 19.36, 20.25, 19.45,
            18.18, 20.59, 19.15, 17.18],
    "AFL": [24.16, 24.46, 23.12, 23.14, 23.24, 21.46, 22.52, 22.67, 22.16, 21.15]}


def league_ppg():
    from gridiron.data import CACHE
    path = CACHE / "fivethirtyeight_nfl_games.csv"
    try:
        if not path.exists():
            CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            pd.read_csv(URL).to_csv(path, index=False)
        g = pd.read_csv(path)
        g = g[(g["playoff"] == 0) & g["season"].between(1932, 1977)].copy()
        g["league"] = "NFL"
        g.loc[g["season"].between(1960, 1969) & g["team1"].isin(AFL_TEAMS), "league"] = "AFL"
        g.loc[g["season"].between(1946, 1949) & g["team1"].isin(AAFC_TEAMS), "league"] = "AAFC"
        g["pts"] = g["score1"] + g["score2"]
        out = g.groupby(["league", "season"]).agg(pts=("pts", "sum"), games=("pts", "size"))
        out["ppg"] = out["pts"] / (2 * out["games"])
        return out["ppg"].unstack(0)
    except Exception:
        nfl = pd.Series(FALLBACK["NFL"], index=range(1932, 1978))
        afl = pd.Series(FALLBACK["AFL"], index=range(1960, 1970))
        return pd.DataFrame({"NFL": nfl, "AFL": afl})


ppg = league_ppg()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax.axvspan(1969.5, 1977.5, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.08, lw=0)
ax.text(1973.5, 26.3, "the scoring\ndrought", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
        style="italic")
nfl = ppg["NFL"].dropna()
afl = ppg["AFL"].dropna()
ax.plot(nfl.index, nfl.values, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=2.0, marker="o", ms=2.6, label="NFL")
ax.plot(afl.index, afl.values, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=2.0, marker="o", ms=2.6, label="AFL (1960–69)")
ax.set_xlim(1930.5, 1978.5)
ax.set_ylim(6, 27)
ax.set_ylabel("points per team per game")
ax.set_xticks(range(1935, 1980, 5))


def note(x, y, text, xt, yt, ha="center"):
    ax.annotate(text, xy=(x, y), xytext=(xt, yt), fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK, ha=ha, va="center",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=3))


note(1932, nfl[1932], "1932: 8.2", 1934.0, 7.2, ha="left")
note(1933, nfl[1933], "1933: pass from anywhere\nbehind the line; hash marks", 1937.0, 9.0, ha="left")
note(1940, nfl[1940], "1940: the T arrives", 1941.5, 12.6, ha="left")
note(1948, nfl[1948], "1948: 23.2", 1944.5, 25.3, ha="center")
note(1960, afl[1960], "AFL outscores the NFL\nin its early seasons", 1955.5, 25.6, ha="center")
note(1972, nfl[1972], "1972: hashes\nmoved in", 1966.0, 16.4, ha="center")
note(1974, nfl[1974], "1974: rule\npackage", 1971.6, 14.6, ha="center")
note(1977, nfl[1977], "1977: head slap banned,\none contact; 17.2", 1973.4, 10.4, ha="center")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.6)
ax.set_yticks(range(8, 27, 4))
ax.set_title("Points per team per game, 1932–1977", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

Read the curve in three pieces. From 1932 to 1948, scoring nearly tripled: the 1933 passing rule, the
end of the incompletion penalty, the T, and platoon football all pushed the same way. Through the 1950s
and '60s it held steady, around 21 or 22 points a game in the NFL and a little more in the AFL, with
offense and defense trading innovations. Then, after the merger, it fell: 19.3 in 1970, 18.2 in 1974,
and 17.2 in 1977, the lowest since 1942. In 1977 no receiver in the NFL gained 1,000
yards.[^ppg] The book calls this the **1970s scoring drought**. (Older writing sometimes borrows
baseball's term "dead-ball era"; it's the same decade.)

The passing numbers tell the same story from the other side. In 1977 NFL teams threw just 25 passes a
game, against 29.4 in 1954; only 42 percent of their plays were passes, and they ran 37.4 times a game,
a modern-era record. A pass gained 6.5 yards per attempt, down from about 7.4 in
1956–65, and from 1970 through 1977 more than five of every hundred passes were intercepted.[^passrate]
Throwing had become both less rewarding and riskier, so teams did less of it.

### Why the defense got ahead

No single cause, but five that reinforced each other.

**1. Receivers could be hit all the way down the field.** Until 1974 a defender could chuck a receiver
(hit or shove him with his hands) anywhere on the field, as often as he liked, until the ball was
thrown. A receiver who has to fight through a linebacker at 5 yards, a safety at 12 and a cornerback all
the way can't run his route on time, and a timing passing game depends on routes run on time.

**2. Pass blockers couldn't use their hands.** Offensive linemen of the era had to keep their hands close
to their chests while pass blocking, and couldn't extend their arms to push a rusher away, while
defensive linemen could use their hands freely, including the *head slap*, a swat to the side of a
blocker's helmet (legal until 1977). Pass protection was a fight with one side's hands tied.

**3. The great four-man lines.** The 4-3 had matured, and the decade's best teams were built on their
defensive lines: the Steelers' "Steel Curtain," the Vikings' "Purple People Eaters," Dallas's Doomsday,
and early in the decade the Rams' "Fearsome Foursome" (Deacon Jones, its most famous member, was traded
after the 1971 season). Four rushers who could win without help let seven defenders cover.[^lines]

**4. Zone coverage grew up.** Defenses had learned to play zones as a team. The best-known version was
the two-deep shell Bud Carson had begun developing as Georgia Tech's head coach and brought to
Pittsburgh in 1972 ([Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)): corners jamming
receivers at the line, safeties over the top, and, in Pittsburgh, a middle linebacker (Jack Lambert,
from 1974) who ran deep down the middle, the ancestor of Tampa 2. The 1976 Steelers allowed 28 points in
their last nine games, with five shutouts.[^steelers76] Zones that are combined with unlimited chucking
are close to airtight.

**5. Offenses played it safe.** When passing is that hard, the sensible strategy is to run, punt and win
the field-position battle, and many coaches did. The game turned into a contest of whose defense would
blink first.

### Why then? What changed around 1970

Notice something odd about that list. Causes 1 and 2 are *old* rules. Defenders had been allowed to
chuck receivers downfield, and blockers had been forbidden to extend their arms, all through the 1950s
and '60s, when the NFL scored 21 or 22 points a game and the AFL more. Rules that didn't change can't by
themselves explain a fall. What they can explain is why the fall, once it started, was so hard to
reverse. So what was new?

- **Zones met the chuck rule.** Against man coverage, a receiver had one defender to beat, and the man
  hitting him was the man covering him. In a team zone, the receiver runs *through* several defenders'
  areas, and under the old rules each of them could hit him on the way. The rule was the same; its value
  to the defense multiplied as defenses moved from man toward zone. That shift is the late-1960s and
  early-'70s story of cause 4 (Carson's Cover 2 reached the NFL in 1972), and it was the defenses'
  answer to the Gillman-style passing that had beaten man coverage in the 1960s.
- **The defensive talent caught up.** The AFL's early scoring edge probably owed something to thin
  defenses in a new league. By 1969 its scoring had fallen back to the NFL's level (the orange line on the chart), and
  after the common draft (from 1967) and the merger, every team drew from the same talent pool. The great
  four-man lines of cause 3 were built in exactly those years.
- **Coaches took the hint.** Once the first two changes made passing riskier, the safe, run-first
  strategy of cause 5 won games (the 1972 Dolphins went 17–0 with it), and winning strategies get copied.

The constants (the chuck rule and the blockers' hands) were the fuel; the new zones and the new
defensive talent were the spark. That's why the cure, when it came, had to change the constants.

New defenses kept coming, too. In 1972 Miami's Bill Arnsparger moved a linebacker around his front in
the package that became the [53 defense](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd), and in 1974 the
New England Patriots and Houston Oilers began using the 3-4 as a base defense, a story [Odd and Hybrid
Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) tells in full.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Miami Dolphins, 1972"}
The only team in NFL history to finish a full season unbeaten and untied, the 1972 Dolphins went 17–0
and beat Washington 14–7 in Super Bowl VII. They did it in the most 1970s way imaginable: with a
dominant running game (Larry Csonka and Mercury Morris both ran for 1,000 yards, a first for two
teammates) and a defense so lacking in stars that it was called the "No-Name Defense." Their starting
quarterback, Bob Griese, broke his leg in the fifth game, and 38-year-old Earl Morrall started most of
the rest of the season.[^dolphins]

**What to notice:** how few passes Miami threw and how rarely it needed to. When defenses rule, the
team that never turns the ball over and never gives up a big play wins. And watch any 1970s
Steelers highlight for the other half of the era: how far downfield defensive backs are still allowed
to hit receivers, and how quickly quarterbacks give up and throw short. That's what the rule-makers
were trying to change.
:::

### The fixes that failed

The league saw the problem early and tried to fix it, three times.

**1972: the hash marks.** The NFL had first painted hash marks in 1933, 10 yards in from each sideline,
and moved them to 20 yards in 1945. In 1972 it moved them in again, to 23 yards, 1 foot, 9 inches
from each sideline, the width of the goalposts. A ball spotted on a hash used to leave the offense a
cramped short side and a vast wide side; now the field was almost symmetrical.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hashes
#| fig-cap: "The 1972 hash-mark change, with the ball on the left hash in both panels (to scale; the field is 53⅓ yards wide). Left, 1945–1971: the hashes were 20 yards in from each sideline, so a play from the hash left 20 yards to the short (boundary) side and 33⅓ yards to the wide (field) side. Right, from 1972: the hashes moved to 23 yards, 1 foot, 9 inches (about 23.6 yards) from each sideline, just 18½ feet apart, leaving about 23.6 yards to the short side and 29.75 to the wide side. More room to the short side meant more room for running plays and quick throws in either direction."
W = 160 / 3


def hash_panel(ax, hash_in, title):
    ax.set_xlim(-1.5, W + 1.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-5.5, 13.0)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), W, 10, fc=style.TURF, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0))
    for yl in (0, 5, 10):
        ax.plot([0, W], [yl, yl], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8 if yl != 5 else 0.5)
    for x in (hash_in, W - hash_in):
        for yy in np.arange(1, 10, 1):
            if yy % 5:
                ax.plot([x, x], [yy - 0.4, yy + 0.4], color=style.INK, lw=1.5)
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((hash_in, 5.0), 1.3, 0.8, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=5))
    for x0, x1, y, txt in [(0, hash_in, -1.6, f"{hash_in:.1f} yd"), (hash_in, W, -1.6, f"{W - hash_in:.1f} yd")]:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x0, y), xytext=(x1, y), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9))
        ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y - 1.5, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK)
    ax.text(hash_in, 11.1, "ball on the hash", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2)
    ax.text(0.0, 12.9, title, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    ax.text(hash_in / 2, 5.0, "short\nside", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2,
            style="italic")
    ax.text((hash_in + W) / 2 + 3.0, 5.0, "wide side", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0,
            color=style.INK_2, style="italic")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 1.95))
hash_panel(axes[0], 20.0, "1945–1971")
hash_panel(axes[1], 70.75 / 3, "From 1972")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.93, bottom=0.02, wspace=0.08)
plt.show()
```

It helped the run more than the pass, and the reason is the sideline. Before 1972, a ball on the hash
left only 20 yards to the short side, and a defense could treat that sideline as an extra defender: a
sweep or an option run that way ran out of room fast, so in practice the offense ran to the wide side
and the defense knew it. With the ball nearly in the middle, a run could go either way with room to
spare, and the defense had to honor both. A pass, which travels over the defense rather than around it,
gained much less: the long throw to the wide side got a few yards shorter, and that was about it. In 1973
Buffalo's O. J. Simpson ran for 2,003 yards, the first **2,000-yard rushing season** in NFL history.
Scoring barely moved.[^hash72]

**1974: the package.** With a rival league (the short-lived World Football League) advertising a more
exciting game, the NFL's competition committee passed its biggest set of changes in decades, aimed, in
its own words, at making long touchdown drives more achievable:[^rules74]

- **The goalposts moved from the goal line to the back of the end zone**, ten yards farther away, so a
  drive that stalled at the 20 was no longer an easy field goal. That sounds like a way to cut scoring,
  and at first it was. The idea was that fewer cheap field-goal tries would mean more fourth-down
  attempts and more drives played out for touchdowns (the same logic, half a century early, as the go-for-it argument in [The Clock, the Two-Minute
  Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)),
  and more room in the end zone for passes now that the posts weren't standing in it.
- **Kickoffs moved back from the 40 to the 35**, so more of them could be returned.
- **A missed field goal went back to the line of scrimmage** (or to the 20 if the kick came from inside
  it), so a long attempt was no longer free.
- **Offensive holding dropped from 15 yards to 10**, and receivers lined up wide could no longer be cut
  at the knees.
- **The first chuck rule**: once a receiver was 3 yards past the line of scrimmage, a defender could
  contact him only once.

That last item introduces this chapter's last term. A [**chuck
rule**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-chuck-rule) is any rule limiting how a defender may hit or
shove a receiver running his route. The 1974 version was sometimes called the "Isaac Curtis rule," after
the fast, slender Cincinnati receiver whom Miami's defense had knocked down as often as it could in a
1973 playoff game; the Bengals' owner, Paul Brown, sat on the rules committee and lobbied for the
change. In 1977 the
league tightened it so that a defender could contact a receiver only once in all, and banned the head
slap.[^rules77]

Look at the chart again and you'll see that 1974, the package's first season, is itself a dip, from
19.4 to 18.2. The goalposts explain it. Field-goal attempts fell from more than 860 in 1973 to 553 in
1974.[^fg74] If about three in five of those lost kicks would have gone in, that is something like 180
field goals, or roughly 1.5 points per team per game, more than the whole 1974 drop. The touchdowns the
committee hoped would replace them came a year later: scoring rose to 20.6 in 1975. Then it fell again,
to 19.2 in 1976 and 17.2 in 1977.

### Why the fixes failed

Look at what the 1972 and 1974 changes touched: where the ball was spotted, where the goalposts stood,
how kicks were returned, how far a penalty walked off. Each was sensible. None changed the basic
arithmetic of a pass play. Under the 1974 rule a defender could still jam a receiver as he left the line
and hit him again once he crossed 3 yards; an offensive lineman still couldn't extend his arms to protect
his quarterback. As long as the receiver couldn't get open on time and the quarterback couldn't stand
in the pocket long enough to wait for him, the passing game that the AFL had proved could win stayed
too risky to build an offense around. The rules had nibbled at the edges of the defense's advantage
without touching its center.

The 1977 rule looks, at first, like the real fix: one contact and no more, plus no head slap. Why did
scoring hit bottom that very season? Because *where* the contact came was still up to the defender. He
could spend it at the line, or he could save it for the moment that hurt most: 15 yards downfield, just
as the receiver planted to make his break. One well-timed hit there wrecks a timed route as surely as
five scattered ones. And the other half of the problem was untouched: banning the head slap took one
weapon from the rushers, but the blockers still couldn't extend their arms.

The changes that finally worked, in 1978, went straight at both halves. Contact with receivers was
allowed only within 5 yards of the line (the [Mel Blount rule](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd)),
so past that point a receiver could run his route untouched and arrive on time; and pass blockers were
allowed to extend their arms and open their hands. That's the next chapter, and the scoring chart turns
upward from there.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the rules are the third player"}
This chapter's history has three actors, not two. Offenses innovate, defenses answer, and the rules
decide which side the board tilts toward. The 1906 pass rules held the forward pass back for a
generation; the 1933 and 1934 changes released it; free substitution made the T a specialist's offense;
and the drought of the 1970s ended only when the league changed the rules of contact. Whenever you read
about a scheme "taking over" the NFL, ask what rule made it possible. You'll ask it again in [Contact
Rules and Penalties as
Strategy](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).
:::

## What survives

Not one of this chapter's formations is a base offense in today's NFL, and almost all of their ideas
are still on the field.

- **The single wing's direct snap** became the shotgun, now the formation of most NFL snaps, and lives
  on in its purest form in the [wildcat](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)
  and in every [direct snap](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) to a running back
  on the goal line. Its spinners and reverses are the ancestors of today's jet sweeps and misdirection.
- **The T's under-center quarterback** never left: it is the base of play-action, and under-center
  snaps rose to about a third of NFL plays in 2025.
- **Paul Brown's organization** (staffs, playbooks, film, sideline play-calling) is simply how football
  is run.
- **The umbrella's idea**, showing one structure and playing another after the snap, is the heart of
  modern disguise and simulated pressure.
- **The 4-3** remains one of the two families of base front, and **the Flex's gap ownership** is how
  every defense now teaches run fits.
- **Gillman's** deep-and-wide passing is the grammar of every passing concept in Part 4.
- **The AFL's** two-point conversion arrived in the NFL in 1994, and its spirit, that you win by
  scoring, won the argument in 1978.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: spot the ancestor"}
Pick one quarter of a game and hunt for the old ideas hiding in modern plays.

- **A direct snap to a running back.** A back alone behind the center, the quarterback split wide or
  gone, maybe an extra lineman on one side: that's the single wing, now called the wildcat. Note
  which side the extra blocker is on and whether the play went there.
- **Someone running across the formation at the snap.** A jet or fly motion is the single wing's
  wingback on a reverse, or the T's man in motion. Watch whether the ball goes with him or the other
  way, like the 1940 Bears' counter.
- **A [buck sweep](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) or a toss with two guards pulling.** That's Lombardi's sweep (and the Wing-T's cousin
  of it). Watch the back: does he cut inside or outside the last block? That's running to daylight.
- **A defensive end who drops into coverage.** When an edge player who lined up on the line turns and
  runs to the flat, you've seen Owen's umbrella move, seventy-five years later.
- **The quarterback under center with two backs behind him.** It's the T's descendant, and in 2025 it
  usually meant a run or a play-action pass.
- **Log it.** Write down each ancestor you spot and what happened on the play. One wildcat, one jet
  motion counter and one dropping end is a good quarter's hunting.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: spot the ancestor"}
Third-and-1 near midfield, 2025. The offense breaks the huddle into this:

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-wildcat
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: a direct-snap look. The running back (R, aqua ring) stands about five yards behind the center; the quarterback (Q) is split wide to the right, off the line. The line is unbalanced: the left tackle (dark ring) has lined up outside the right tackle, beside the tight end (Y). Before the snap, a second back (H) starts in motion from the left (dashed). Defense: E = end, T = tackle, S/M/W = linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS/SS = safeties."
wc_off = check_legal([
    OL("LG", -OL_SPLIT), OL("C", 0.0, "C"), OL("RG", OL_SPLIT), OL("RT", 2 * OL_SPLIT), OL("LT", 3 * OL_SPLIT),
    P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4 * OL_SPLIT + 1.0, "Y"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0),
    P("RB", "RB", -5.0, 0.0, "R"), P("H", "RB", -5.0, -4.5, "H"), P("QB", "QB", OFF_BALL, 13.0, "Q"),
    P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, -7.5, "Z")])
wc_def = base43_60s({"WDE": dict(w=-3.2), "WDT": dict(w=-0.9), "SDT": dict(w=3.0), "SDE": dict(w=5.9),
                     "SAM": dict(d=3.6, w=8.6), "MIKE": dict(d=4.4, w=1.6), "WILL": dict(d=4.4, w=-2.6),
                     "LCB": dict(w=-12.0), "RCB": dict(w=13.0, d=6.5), "FS": dict(d=11.5, w=-1.0),
                     "SS": dict(d=7.5, w=-7.5)})
q1 = Play(wc_off, wc_def, los=50, to_go=1)
q1.motion("H", to=(-4.5, -1.7))
q1.highlight("RB", color=BACK_RING)
q1.highlight("LT", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw_play(q1, lateral=(-16.5, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 14.0))
plt.show()
```

**What old formation is this, and where do you expect the ball to go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**It's the single wing in modern clothes**, the look broadcasters call the wildcat. Every piece has an
ancestor: the direct snap to a runner five yards deep (the single-wing tailback), the unbalanced line
with an extra lineman on one side (the single wing's four-men-to-one-side line), and a second back
crossing the formation at the snap (the wingback's reverse, or the 1940 T's man in motion).

**The likeliest play is a run to the strong side, the right.** On third-and-1 the offense wants a yard.
To the right of the center it has three linemen and a tight end, a blocker for each of the four
defenders on that side, with the motion man arriving as a fifth: the single wing's off-tackle power,
with more blockers than defenders at the point of attack.

**The counter-threat is the motion man.** If the defense slides right to stop the power, the ball can go
to H on his sweep, or the runner can fake to him and keep it, exactly the spinner-and-reverse logic that
kept 1930s defenses honest. And because the quarterback split wide is still an eligible receiver, one
defender has to cover him, which takes a man out of the box. What makes the modern version a gimmick
rather than a base offense is the pass: few running backs can throw well enough to make the defense
respect it, which is why the single wing's triple-threat tailback mattered so much.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: October 22, 1961"}
San Francisco's shotgun has carried the 49ers to a 4–1 start, including shutouts of 49–0 and 35–0. The 49ers line up in it against the
Bears: quarterback about seven yards deep, receivers spread. The Bears' middle linebacker, Bill George,
has walked up from his usual spot.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-shotgun
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the 1961 shotgun (an illustrative alignment) against the Bears' 4-3, with middle linebacker Bill George (M, orange ring) walked up onto the line, head-up on the center. The quarterback (Q) is about seven yards deep; one back (F) stands beside him; the other backs and ends are spread. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, S/W = outside linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS/SS = safeties."
sg_off = check_legal(line5() + [
    P("QB", "QB", -7.0, 0.0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", -5.5, 2.2, "F"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0),
    P("H", "HB", OFF_BALL, -7.5, "H"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 6.5, "Y"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.5)])
sg_def = base43_60s({"MIKE": dict(d=1.0, w=0.0), "WDT": dict(w=-2.2), "SDT": dict(w=2.4), "WDE": dict(w=-4.4),
                     "SDE": dict(w=4.6), "SAM": dict(d=4.6, w=6.2), "WILL": dict(d=4.6, w=-5.6),
                     "LCB": dict(w=-14.0), "RCB": dict(w=13.5), "FS": dict(d=12.5, w=-7.0),
                     "SS": dict(d=10.0, w=7.5)})
q2 = Play(sg_off, sg_def, los=40, to_go=10)
q2.highlight("MIKE", color=KEY_RING)
fld = draw_play(q2, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.5, 15.0))
plt.show()
```

**What is the Bears' plan, and why does it work against this formation in particular?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Rush the center.** In the shotgun the center has the hardest job on the field: he must look between
his legs, throw a seven-yard snap accurately, and only then lift his head to block. A defender lined up
directly over him gets a head start every time. With George on the center, either the center loses the
one-on-one, or a guard has to help, and then someone else is free.

**Why it works here:** the 1961 shotgun had almost no running threat to punish an aggressive rush. A
quarterback seven yards deep with a single back beside him can't hand off quickly or threaten a quick
dive, so the defense could commit to the pass rush. With pressure up the middle arriving before
receivers spread across a wide field could get open, the 49ers had nowhere to go: the Bears won 31–0,
and Hickey retired the formation. The modern shotgun survives because offenses solved both problems:
quarterbacks set up about five yards deep, not seven, and there is a real run game (and the RPO) from
it, so a defense that sends everyone at the center pays for it.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-8, 1977"}
Third-and-8 at the offense's own 35, third quarter, 1977. The offense is in split backs with a tight end
and two wide receivers; the defense is a two-deep 4-3 with both cornerbacks squeezed up tight on the
receivers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1977
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: third-and-8 in 1977. Offense: split backs (H and F), tight end Y, receivers X and Z. Defense: a 4-3 with two deep safeties (FS, SS) about 12 yards deep and both cornerbacks (C, orange rings) pressed tight on the receivers at the line."
q3_def = base43_60s({"LCB": dict(d=1.2, w=-13.4), "RCB": dict(d=1.2, w=12.0), "FS": dict(d=12.5, w=-8.5),
                     "SS": dict(d=12.5, w=8.5)})
q3_off = pro_set_red()
q3_off = [q.moved(w=12.5) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in q3_off]
q3 = Play(q3_off, q3_def, los=45, to_go=8)
q3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", color=KEY_RING)
fld = draw_play(q3, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 16.0))
plt.show()
```

**What are the defense's advantages under the 1977 rules, and what is the offense's most sensible
call?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The defense's advantages are the rulebook's.** Those pressed corners can jam the receivers at the line,
and under the 1977 rule they get one legal contact on each, used right where it hurts the timing most.
Seven defenders are in coverage behind them in a two-deep zone, the safeties over the top. Up front,
four rushers can use their hands freely (the head slap is gone in 1977, but blockers still can't extend
their arms), so the quarterback doesn't have long.

**The offense's sensible call is something short and safe**: a quick pass to a back or the tight end
underneath the zone, or a draw that punishes the four rushers for charging, and then a punt if it comes
up short. A 15-yard throw against this defense in 1977 asks a jammed receiver to get open in time
behind a protection that can't hold up. That's the drought in one snap: on third-and-8, the most
rational play was to *try* for a first down without risking an interception, and punt. A year later,
with contact limited to 5 yards and blockers allowed to extend their arms, the same third-and-8 became
a throwing down again.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Football's history is action, reaction and rules.** Offenses innovate, defenses answer, and the
  rule-makers tilt the board. The forward pass, legal from 1906, didn't matter until the rules stopped
  punishing it (1933–34).
- **The single wing was built for power and deception from a direct snap; the T beat it with speed and a
  specialist passer.** The 1940 Bears' 73–0 made the switch, and platoon football (permanent in the NFL
  from 1950) made the specialist possible.
- **Paul Brown turned football into a profession**: full-time staffs, playbooks, film, measurable
  athletes, and plays called from the sideline. Every modern staff runs on his model.
- **The 4-3 was the defense's answer to the pro passing game.** Owen's umbrella showed a 6-1-4 and played a
  4-1-6; Bill George stood up in the middle; Landry built the 4-3 in 1956 and the Flex in the 1960s to
  take away Lombardi's daylight by giving every gap an owner.
- **Gillman and the AFL proved the passing game could win**, using the whole field, deep and wide, and
  the merged league inherited their ideas.
- **The 1970s drought came from rules that let defenses hit receivers and hobbled pass blockers**, plus
  great four-man lines and team zone coverage. The 1972 hash marks and the 1974 package changed the
  margins of the game, not the arithmetic of a pass play, so scoring fell to 17.2 in 1977.

The early restrictions: "The Early History of Football's Forward Pass," *Smithsonian Magazine*: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-early-history-of-footballs-forward-pass-78015237 (no pass across the line within five yards of the center; an untouched pass that hit the ground went to the defense); "From Turnover to Touchback: The Punitive Era of the Early Forward Pass," *Pigskin Dispatch*: https://pigskindispatch.com/from-turnover-to-touchback-the-punitive-era-of-the-early-forward-pass/ (historian Timothy Brown: incompletions were turnovers in 1906 and became a 15-yard penalty in 1907; a pass caught in the end zone was a touchback). Sources differ on exactly which restriction applied in which year (the 20-yard limit on a pass's length appears in some 1906 accounts and is restated in 1910), which is why the text gives the rules without dating each one.

The 1912 removal of the 20-yard limit on a pass's length, and the end-zone pass: Pigskin Dispatch, "From Turnover to Touchback" (cited in the 1906 note), and Smithsonian, "The Early History of Football's Forward Pass" (same note).

On the slimmer ball: "Forward pass," Wikipedia (narrower balls from the 1920s onward made spiral throws easier).

[^singlewing]: "Single-wing formation," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-wing_formation (Warner's "Carlisle formation" at Carlisle by 1907; unbalanced line with two linemen on one side of the center and four on the other, made by "moving the off-side guard or tackle to the strong side"; "designed to place double-team blocks at the point of attack"; tailback, fullback, blocking back called the quarterback, and wingback; the spinner and buck-lateral series; the name from the wing back's shape). The NFL's in-between years: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "General history chronology, 1940 to 1959": https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/general-history-chronology-1940-to-1959/ (free substitution adopted April 7, 1943, and renewed for 1944 and 1945; withdrawn in 1946, with substitutions limited to no more than three men at a time; free substitution adopted for one year in 1949; "unlimited free substitution was restored" on January 20, 1950).

[^brown]: "Paul Brown," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Brown (Massillon; Ohio State's 1942 national title; four AAFC titles 1946–49; 35–10 over the Eagles in the Browns' first NFL game; the 1950, 1954 and 1955 NFL titles; full-time assistants; playbooks and tests; first to use film to scout opponents; intelligence tests; the 40-yard dash at Ohio State in 1941; the draw play's 1946 origin; Motley and Willis in 1946); "Paul Brown," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/paul-brown/ ; "Otto Graham," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/otto-graham/ (ten seasons, ten championship games). The punt-cover rationale is the usual account (Wikipedia's article gives it); Mike Brown doubts "the punt part" and says his father chose 40 yards "because he thought that was the longest anyone had to run on a football field for the most part": Geoff Hobson, "A fast look at the 40," Bengals.com (2017): https://bengals.com/news/a-fast-look-at-the-40-18598225 .

[^radio]: "Chuck Noll," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Noll (Browns 1953–1959; one of Brown's "messenger guards," who Brown said soon "could have called the plays himself"); "Ratterman's radio helmet," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/news/ratterman-s-radio-helmet (1956; spotted by the Lions in a preseason game; banned by Commissioner Bert Bell); the 1994 adoption of helmet radios is from the same history.

[^eagles50]: "Top moments No. 25: Browns defeat Eagles in 1950 without throwing a single pass," Cleveland Browns: https://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/top-moments-no-25-browns-defeat-eagles-in-1950-without-throwing-a-single-pass (September 16 opener, 35–10; Graham 346 yards and three touchdowns; Neale's basketball remark in several wordings; the December 3 rematch, 13–7, with no official pass attempt, and "no other NFL team in 71 years since has completed a game with zero pass attempts"); "1950 Cleveland Browns season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_Cleveland_Browns_season (two passes thrown, both called back on penalties; no team since has failed to attempt a pass); "1950 Philadelphia Eagles season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_Philadelphia_Eagles_season .

[^owen]: "Steve Owen (American football)," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Owen_(American_football) (Giants head coach from 1930 to 1953; titles in 1934 and 1938; the umbrella defense against the 1950 Browns; the Giants won 6–0 and 17–13 before losing the playoff); "4–3 defense," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4%E2%80%933_defense (quoting Owen, *My Kind of Football*, 1952, p. 183: a "6–1–4 basic formation" that on many plays was "4–1–6 in reality"; Landry explained and taught it); "1950 New York Giants season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_New_York_Giants_season (6–0 on October 1, the Browns' first shutout; the 8–3 playoff loss); "1950 Cleveland Browns season," Wikipedia (the American Conference playoff, December 17, 1950, at Cleveland Stadium: two Lou Groza field goals and a safety to a Giants field goal, 8–3).

[^george]: "Bill George," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/bill-george/ ("no one can swear" which middle guard first dropped off the line, but George is the most popular choice; he began doing it in 1954); "Bill George (linebacker)," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_George_(linebacker) .

[^landry43]: "Tom Landry," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/tom-landry/ (Giants player-coach 1954–55 and defensive coach 1956–59; Cowboys head coach from 1960); "4–3 defense," Wikipedia (Landry the first to make the 4–3 a base defense, in 1956; the league converted the next season); "Sam Huff," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Huff (the rookie middle linebacker of 1956; *The Violent World of Sam Huff*, a CBS special broadcast in October 1960 as an episode of the Cronkite-hosted *The Twentieth Century*).

[^flex]: "4–3 defense," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4%E2%80%933_defense (the Flex developed to counter option blocking, in which linemen take defenders whichever way they go and "the running back would then patiently run to daylight"; two linemen flexed off the line to read; built to use Bob Lilly's quickness); Paul Zimmerman, "Ten Most Revolutionary Defensive Players," *Sports Illustrated*, Nov. 21, 2006: https://www.si.com/uncategorized/2006/11/21/21ten-most-revolutionary-defensive-players (Lilly "spearheaded" the Flex); "Is there any way to explain football's most confusing… defense?", *D Magazine*, August 1987: https://www.dmagazine.com/publications/d-magazine/1987/august/is-there-any-wayto-explain-footballs-most-confusing-convoluted-intellectually-taxing-perhaps-no-longer-so-great-defense/ (two linemen set back about a yard, varying with the offense's formation; players taught exact steps). Sources give its first use as 1964, 1965 or 1966 and the flex distance as anything from two feet to a yard; the Pro Football Hall of Fame's Landry biography says only "the 1960s," and the most specific account (Pro Football Researchers forum, citing *D Magazine*) has it used occasionally in 1964 and regularly from 1965.

[^icebowl]: "1967 NFL Championship Game," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_NFL_Championship_Game (December 31, 1967, Lambeau Field; −13°F at kickoff, about −15°F at game time by another figure in the same article; third-and-goal at the two-foot line with 16 seconds left and no timeouts; Starr's sneak behind Kramer and Bowman's double-team of Jethro Pugh, scoring with 13 seconds remaining; Packers 21–17); "1966 NFL Championship Game," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NFL_Championship_Game (Green Bay 34, Dallas 27).

[^gillman]: "Sid Gillman," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sid_Gillman (cut football clips from newsreels at his family's theater; Rams 1955–59; Chargers 1960–69; 1963 AFL title, 51–10 over Boston; Al Davis: "It had been thought of as vertical, the length of the field, but Sid also thought of it as horizontal"; coaching descendants Davis, Noll, Walsh and Vermeil, with Coryell studying his methods); "Sid Gillman," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/sid-gillman/ .

[^chargers63]: "1963 American Football League Championship Game," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1963_American_Football_League_Championship_Game (January 5, 1964, Balboa Stadium, San Diego; Chargers 51, Patriots 10; Lincoln "rushed for 206 yards on 13 carries, led the team with 123 yards in receiving").

[^afl]: "American Football League," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League (founded August 1959 by Lamar Hunt and others; eight teams in 1960; the two-point conversion, adopted by the NFL in 1994; names on jerseys and the scoreboard clock as official time; equal sharing of the ABC television money; the NBC contract of January 1964, \$36 million, from 1965; Namath's signing on January 2, 1965, for \$427,000; merger announced June 8, 1966; the AFC formed in 1970 from the ten AFL teams plus the Colts, Browns and Steelers; Super Bowl III 16–7). The 1960–64 scoring gap is the course calculation in the points note.

[^stram]: "Hank Stram," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Stram (Texans/Chiefs 1960–1974; AFL titles 1962, 1966, 1969; the moving pocket and triple-stack defense; first pro coach to use the I-formation and two tight ends; recruited heavily from historically Black colleges; "In the Super Bowl, Stram became the first professional football coach to wear a microphone": "Just keep matriculatin' the ball down the field, boys"); "Super Bowl IV," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_IV (Chiefs 23, Vikings 7, January 11, 1970). Buchanan (Grambling) and Lanier (Morgan State): Pro Football Hall of Fame player pages.

[^shotgun]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "The Shotgun Formation": https://www.profootballhof.com/news/the-shotgun-formation (first used November 27, 1960, 30–22 over the Colts; "really just a new version of an old formation"; Brodie, Kilmer and Waters rotated in 1961; a 4–1 start including 49–0 over Detroit and 35–0 over the Rams; on October 22, 1961, the Bears won 31–0 after Bill George "moved up to the line of scrimmage" and the Bears penetrated "by attacking the center"; Hickey then retired the formation; Landry's Cowboys later revived it). The seven-yard depth is from the same history of the formation as told in [Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).

[^ppg]: Course calculation from FiveThirtyEight's file of every NFL game's final score since 1920 (`nfl_games.csv`, https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/nfl-elo-game), regular-season games only: total points ÷ (2 × games) per season. AFL teams in 1960–69 are separated by franchise; AAFC games of 1946–49 are excluded. The 1977 value (17.2, the lowest since 1942) and the absence of a 1,000-yard receiver match "1977 NFL season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_NFL_season . Cross-check any single season against Pro Football Reference's league averages.

[^hash72]: The hash-mark history (20 yards from 1945; 70 feet 9 inches from 1972) is sourced in [The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd); "1972 NFL season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_NFL_season . Simpson's 2,003 yards in 1973: "O. J. Simpson," Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/o-j-simpson/ .

[^rules74]: "1974 NFL season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_NFL_season (goalposts to the end line; kickoffs from the 35; missed field goals returned to the line of scrimmage or the 20, "whichever is farther from" the defense's goal line; holding from 15 to 10 yards; no blocks below the waist on receivers aligned two or more yards outside the tackles; one contact after the receiver is 3 yards past the line; the competition committee's aim of making long touchdown drives more achievable, and the WFL's influence).

[^rules77]: "1977 NFL season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_NFL_season (head slap outlawed; "Defenders are only permitted to make contact with receivers once"; 17.2 points per team per game). Gasper, "How wide receivers have evolved in the NFL," *Boston Globe*, Sept. 4, 2013: https://www.bostonglobe.com/sports/2013/09/04/how-wide-receivers-have-evolved-nfl/akAnTGNJaS7OrVnjAbbN6J/story.html .
